Offers practical tuning with competitive runtime, though performance varies across evaluated datasets.
papers.selection_reason: Robust point cloud registration with truncated Lp functions; directly relevant to 3D geometric perception.
papers.title: Robust Single-Parameter Point Cloud Registration using Truncated Lp Functions
papers.tldr: TLP enables robust point cloud registration with one tunable parameter by using truncated $L_p$ functions and GPU-accelerated hypothesis evaluation.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a promising approach for fast, high-quality novel-view rendering. However, its large parameter size remains a bottleneck for storage and transmission. We propose RacerGS, a compact 3DGS compression framework that achieves scene reconstruction at significantly reduced storage sizes with preserved fidelity. To obtain compact and spatially coherent features, we design a hash projection model that projects the anchor hash encodings into compact context features. Additionally, we introduce a FiLM-modulated autoregressive GRU context model that utilizes causal dependencies among anchor feature groups and uses recurrent hidden states to refine entropy-model parameters, improving bitrate efficiency. Furthermore, we adaptively entropy-code quantized anchor-attribute residuals relative to their context-predicted means, leveraging spatial consistency to reduce symbol entropy. Overall, RacerGS achieves more than 150x compression over vanilla 3DGS and 28x over Scaffold-GS, while providing comparable rendering quality. Extensive experiments across five datasets demonstrate that RacerGS outperforms prior 3DGS compression methods in both storage reduction and rate-distortion performance.
authors: Wenqing Wang, Huimin Zeng, Yun Fu
bullets: Addresses the large storage and transmission cost of 3DGS.
Projects anchor hash encodings into compact, spatially coherent context features.
Uses a FiLM-modulated autoregressive GRU to model causal dependencies and refine entropy parameters.
Entropy-codes quantized anchor-attribute residuals relative to context-predicted means.
Reports over 150× compression versus vanilla 3DGS and 28× versus Scaffold-GS, with comparable quality across five datasets.
papers.selection_reason: 3D Gaussian Splatting compression via autoregressive context and entropy coding; relevant to 3D vision and storage efficiency.
papers.title: RacerGS: Residual-Autoregressive Context for 3D Gaussian Splatting Compression
papers.tldr: RacerGS compresses 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes using spatial context and residual entropy coding, achieving substantial storage reduction while preserving rendering quality.

papers.abstract: Scalable 3D Gaussian Splatting allows one scene representation to serve different Gaussian-count budgets, yet its quality-budget curve may lag behind models optimized separately for each budget. Reducing the number of Gaussians changes both the selected members and the reconstruction tasks carried by the survivors; parameters inherited from a high-budget model may fit a low-budget representation poorly. We propose ParetoGS, which describes member changes and parameter evolution with a small set of adapted budget anchors and decodes intermediate budgets without separate optimization at every requested count. ParetoGS alternates pruning and fixed-member adaptation to build nested anchors with persistent identities, and encodes their parameter changes relative to the full model in a compact residual atlas. At decoding, it interpolates the states of shared members and gradually introduces the rendering contributions of new members, connecting sparse anchors into a continuous-budget representation. Across 13 scenes, ParetoGS attains better average PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS with fewer Gaussians than the compared prefix methods at 10% of each method's own full model. From a shared full model, it also outperforms FlexGS-imp at its trained 1%, 5%, and 10% budgets and NanoGS-imp at the 1% and 0.1% budgets. On Garden, its non-anchor quality approaches an empirical reference from independently optimized GNS models at higher retention ratios and exceeds it at some lower-budget points. Across 13 scenes, encoding reduces mean additional state from 390.0 to 85.7 MB with an average PSNR change of 0.01 dB. Project page: https://xiaobin2001.github.io/ParetoGS-Web/
authors: Xiaobin Deng, Changyu Diao, Min Li, Duanqing Xu
bullets: Addresses quality degradation when pruning a high-budget Gaussian model for lower budgets, where surviving parameters may no longer fit well.
Builds nested, persistent-identity anchors through alternating pruning and fixed-member adaptation.
Stores parameter changes in a compact residual atlas and decodes intermediate budgets by interpolating shared members and gradually adding new members.
Across 13 scenes, improves average PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS over prefix methods at 10% retention and outperforms several budget-trained baselines at selected budgets.
Reduces mean additional encoding state from 390.0 MB to 85.7 MB with only a 0.01 dB average PSNR change.
papers.selection_reason: Continuous-budget 3D Gaussian Splatting with pruning and compact residual encoding; relevant to 3D representation and efficiency.
papers.title: ParetoGS: High-Quality Continuous-Budget 3D Gaussian Splatting with Sparse Adapted Anchors
papers.tldr: ParetoGS enables high-quality, continuously adjustable 3D Gaussian Splatting budgets using sparse adapted anchors and interpolation instead of optimizing every Gaussian count separately.

papers.abstract: High-resolution 3D Gaussian Splatting training increases pixel and Gaussian-tile intersection counts, expanding rasterization caches that coexist with projection and gradient state at peak memory. A complete-view update aggregates gradients across the view; each region's forward and backward caches can be released after its contribution is collected. BoundedGS separates rasterization and projection backward passes and bounds the active local rasterization working set according to its measured load. Candidate-indexed projection and compact gradient storage address the view-level peaks exposed by this change, while CPU-assisted structure rebuilding and bounded image supply manage resources outside rendering. In a resolution sweep at a fixed count of about 6M Gaussians, the measured rendering working set stays within 1.073-1.077 GiB from 1K to 16K; at 11K, a warm pass takes 19.79 seconds versus 21.76 for full-frame execution. Across five native 5K outdoor scenes, full training reduces the mean rendering working set from 9.97 to 1.76 GiB (82.3%), retains similar reconstruction quality, and shortens training time from 36.7 to 33.9 minutes. Project page: https://xiaobin2001.github.io/BoundedGS-Web/
authors: Xiaobin Deng, Changyu Diao, Min Li, Duanqing Xu
bullets: High-resolution 3DGS exceeds memory limits because rasterization caches grow alongside projection and gradient state.
It separates rasterization from projection backpropagation and limits the active rasterization working set using measured load.
Candidate-indexed projection, compact gradients, CPU-assisted rebuilding, and bounded image supply control additional memory use.
At roughly 6M Gaussians, rendering memory remains nearly constant at 1.073–1.077 GiB from 1K to 16K resolution.
Across five native 5K outdoor scenes, rendering memory drops 82.3% while quality remains similar and training becomes faster.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-efficient high-resolution 3D Gaussian Splatting training; reduces memory footprint and fits efficient AI and 3D vision.
papers.title: BoundedGS: Memory-Efficient High-Resolution Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: BoundedGS enables memory-efficient high-resolution 3D Gaussian Splatting by bounding rasterization memory while preserving reconstruction quality and improving training time.

papers.abstract: Spatial localization of surgical instruments through bounding-box annotations is a foundational component of surgical scene understanding, supporting detection, tracking, interaction analysis, and grounded vision-language applications. Yet existing annotations often cover selected frames, video subsets, or dataset variants rather than complete procedures. Manual extension is time-consuming and expert-dependent. Additionally, weakly supervised and detector-based pseudo-labels require task-specific training and may be imprecise. In this study, we design a scalable MLLM-based annotation framework that converts surgical frames and existing instrument-presence labels into accurate bounding boxes, and systematically analyze its reliability, cost, and design sensitivity. We instantiate the framework using six MLLMs and a multi-call configuration on laparoscopic cholecystectomy in Cholec80. Using a carefully designed stratification scheme, two annotators independently label 1,000 frames, and an expert surgeon reviews one annotation set to establish the reference. Results show that instrument-set F1 ranges from 88.2 to 92.7,whereas mIoU ranges from 0.180 to 0.735, showing that comparable recognition can conceal large localization differences. A structured multi-stage annotation pipeline achieves 0.784 mIoU, compared with 0.735 for the best single-call baseline and 0.814 human-human agreement. Using the best accuracy pipeline, we create and publicly release a spatial extension of Cholec80 comprising 285,977 bounding boxes across all 184,498 annotated frames from the 80 videos. The annotations and human references are made available on GitHub
authors: Mohamed Hamdy, Muraam Abdel-Ghani, Fatmaelzahraa Ahmed, Sifna Nasar, Mariam Ahmed, Khalid Al-Jalham, Abdulaziz Al-Ali, Shidin Balakrishnan
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited coverage of manually annotated surgical bounding boxes.
Evaluates six MLLMs and multi-call annotation designs on laparoscopic cholecystectomy frames from Cholec80.
Shows that similar instrument recognition F1 can hide substantial localization differences, with mIoU ranging from 0.180 to 0.735.
A structured multi-stage pipeline reaches 0.784 mIoU, approaching human-human agreement of 0.814.
Releases 285,977 bounding boxes covering all 184,498 annotated frames across 80 videos.
papers.selection_reason: MLLM-based framework converting presence labels to bounding boxes; directly relevant to multimodal LLMs and spatial localization.
papers.title: From Presence Labels to Bounding Boxes: Can Multimodal Large Language Models Scale Surgical Instrument Localization?
papers.tldr: A scalable multimodal-LLM pipeline converts surgical instrument-presence labels into bounding boxes, achieving near-human localization quality and enabling a large public spatial extension of Cholec80.

papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly being used in different stages of scientific knowledge production, including the suggestion of references. These models can operate at different levels of reasoning effort and provide summaries of their reasoning processes. This raises two questions: Does increasing reasoning effort improve the verifiability of generated references, and do the resulting reasoning summaries reveal how the model's behavior changes with greater effort? We examined summaries from GPT-5.5 as it generated scholarly references for 1,000 papers under paired low- and high-effort settings. Generated references were matched to external bibliographic records, and reasoning summaries were scored for four predefined features and explored for additional features discovered by GPT-5.5. High effort increased the mean paper-level resolver-verified reference rate from 78.3% to 84.8%, and produced longer reasoning summaries. All four predefined features received higher scores under high effort. The discovered features changed less uniformly: some appeared equally often in both conditions, whereas others were more common under high effort. Within each effort condition, neither feature set showed a consistent increase in verification rates with higher scores.
authors: Melika Mobini, Andres Algaba, Vincent Ginis
bullets: The study compares low- and high-effort GPT-5.5 reference generation for 1,000 papers.
References were checked against external bibliographic records using resolver verification.
High effort increased the mean paper-level verification rate from 78.3% to 84.8%.
All four predefined reasoning-summary features scored higher with high effort, while discovered features changed unevenly.
Within either effort condition, higher feature scores did not consistently correspond to higher verification rates.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the impact of reasoning effort on reference verifiability and reasoning summaries in GPT-5.5, providing insights into model behavior.
papers.title: Higher Reasoning Effort Improves Reference Verifiability and Changes Reasoning Summaries in GPT-5.5
papers.tldr: Higher reasoning effort made GPT-5.5’s generated scholarly references more verifiable and produced longer, systematically different reasoning summaries.

papers.abstract: Modern surgical AI increasingly requires multimodal understanding rather than isolated perception, yet existing datasets remain largely limited to single-task supervision such as recognition or templated question answering. Current medical VQA resources often rely on synthetic templates, lack natural descriptive supervision, or provide sparse annotations that hinder reasoning about spatial relations and procedural context. We introduce MIS-VQA, a surgical vision-language dataset generated through an annotation-driven pipeline that converts heterogeneous surgical annotations into structured textual scene representations. Using EndoVis18 and CholecT50, we transform phase, instrument, interaction, triplet, and segmentation labels into unified contexts that guide large language models to generate clinically coherent question-answer pairs. MIS-VQA supports four response types-concise and detailed descriptions, perception-level grounding, and multi-step reasoning-enabling hierarchical evaluation from atomic visual grounding to compositional reasoning. To address annotation sparsity, we incorporate confidence-filtered segmentation and cross-annotation consistency checks, enabling spatially grounded supervision at scale. MIS-VQA establishes a unified benchmark for surgical vision-language understanding with spatial supervision and multi-tier reasoning evaluation. To demonstrate its utility, we introduce LLaVA-SurgXpert, a family of surgical vision-language models with visual encoders to analyze how visual representations influence multimodal reasoning. Experiments show consistent improvements over existing surgical VQA baselines while revealing capability gaps between perceptual grounding and higher-level reasoning hidden in prior benchmarks.
authors: Mohamed Hamdy, Iheb Zouari, Fatmaelzahraa Ahmed, Muraam Abdel-Ghani, Muhammed Arsalan, Ponnuthurai Suganthan, Khalid Al-Jalham, Abdulaziz Al-Ali, Shidin Balakrishnan
bullets: Addresses limitations of existing surgical VQA datasets, including synthetic questions, sparse annotations, and weak procedural or spatial supervision.
Builds unified scene contexts from phase, instrument, interaction, triplet, and segmentation annotations in EndoVis18 and CholecT50.
Provides four response types: concise and detailed descriptions, perception-level grounding, and multi-step reasoning.
Uses confidence-filtered segmentation and cross-annotation consistency checks to scale spatially grounded supervision.
Introduces LLaVA-SurgXpert models and reports improvements over existing surgical VQA baselines, while exposing gaps between grounding and higher-level reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Surgical vision-language dataset and MLLM family with spatial grounding and multi-step reasoning; relevant to multimodal LLMs and spatial understanding.
papers.title: MIS-VQA: An Annotation-Driven Surgical Vision-Language Dataset for Complex Surgical Understanding
papers.tldr: MIS-VQA turns diverse surgical annotations into a structured vision-language benchmark for evaluating both spatial grounding and multi-step clinical reasoning.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) enables flow-matching models to acquire complementary capabilities from specialized teachers through supervision on student-generated trajectories. However, different evaluation dimensions, such as aesthetics and OCR accuracy, and different tasks, such as image generation and editing, emphasize different aspects of the denoising process, suggesting that their effective supervision may occur at different stages. Existing methods typically select supervision states from predefined timestep distributions, which may overlook these phase-dependent differences and incur unnecessary computational overhead. This motivates two critical timing decisions: when to adaptively query teachers for effective supervision based on the evolving generative process, and when to skip the remaining rollout to avoid redundant computation. In this paper, we introduce PhaseOPD, a phase-aware query-and-skip framework that identifies generative phases online from revisions of predicted-clean latents, using existing student velocity predictions without additional model evaluations. For each task-assigned teacher, PhaseOPD selects a supervision state based on its phase preference and skips the unused rollout suffix once all query decisions are finalized, preserving the single-query velocity-distillation objective. On SD3.5-M, PhaseOPD executes only 5.56 of 16 rollout positions per local batch, reducing training time by 41.3% relative to DanceOPD while improving Aesthetic, GenEval, and OCR scores.
authors: Renye Yan, Junyi Zhan, Jikang Cheng, Wei Peng
bullets: Different tasks and evaluation goals may need teacher supervision at different denoising stages.
The framework identifies phases online from changes in predicted-clean latents, reusing student velocity predictions without extra model evaluations.
Task-specific teachers are queried at preferred phases, while unnecessary rollout suffixes are skipped after query decisions are complete.
On SD3.5-M, it uses 5.56 of 16 rollout positions per local batch and reduces training time by 41.3% versus DanceOPD.
It also improves Aesthetic, GenEval, and OCR scores in the reported setting.
papers.selection_reason: Adaptive query-and-skip in flow-matching distillation reduces training computation, fitting the efficient-AI scope of reducing compute.
papers.title: Timing Matters Twice: When to Query and When to Skip in Flow-Matching On-Policy Distillation
papers.tldr: PhaseOPD makes on-policy distillation more efficient by adaptively choosing when to query teachers and when to stop rollouts based on the evolving generation phase.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary instance segmentation (OVIS) provides a promising solution for marine perception by recognizing and segmenting categories beyond predefined label spaces. Existing OVIS methods usually rely on vision-language alignment, where visual region features are matched with textual category embeddings to recognize both seen and unseen classes. However, this alignment assumption becomes fragile in underwater environments. Color attenuation, scattering, turbidity, and low contrast distort visual appearance, causing region features to deviate from their corresponding semantic concepts. As a result, the similarity between degraded visual features and textual classifiers becomes unreliable, which particularly weakens the recognition of unseen underwater categories that cannot be corrected by category-specific supervision. To address these issues, we propose GeoPrompt, a geometry-conditioned prompt learning framework for underwater open-vocabulary instance segmentation. Our key insight is that geometric structure is more stable than visual appearance in degraded underwater scenes. Specifically, GeoPrompt introduces a geometry-guided visual adaptation module (GVAM) to extract depth-derived structural priors and inject them into multi-scale visual features. It further develops a geometry-conditioned prompt learning (GCPL) that generates geometry-aware textual classifiers from structural representations. These geometry-aware classifiers are integrated with fixed and image-conditioned textual classifiers to improve open-vocabulary semantic alignment. Experiments on the MARIS-OpenIS benchmark show that GeoPrompt achieves state-of-the-art performance and brings consistent improvements on underwater open-vocabulary instance segmentation.
authors: Shanshan Han, Yuxi Wang, Can Qin, Yujie Chen, Cong Pan, Haitao Li, Guoqiang Zhong
bullets: Underwater degradation distorts visual features, making text-based recognition—especially for unseen categories—unreliable.
The method extracts depth-derived structural priors and injects them into multi-scale visual features.
It generates geometry-aware textual classifiers and combines them with fixed and image-conditioned classifiers.
Experiments on MARIS-OpenIS report state-of-the-art performance with consistent improvements.
papers.selection_reason: Geometry-conditioned prompt learning injects depth-derived structural priors into vision-language segmentation, fitting geometry-aware multimodal models.
papers.title: GeoPrompt: Geometry-Conditioned Prompt Learning for Underwater Open-Vocabulary Instance Segmentation
papers.tldr: GeoPrompt improves underwater open-vocabulary instance segmentation by using stable geometric cues to strengthen vision-language alignment.

papers.abstract: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) of LLMs suffers from catastrophic forgetting, and prevailing mitigation strategies struggle to reconcile the plasticity-stability dilemma. To address this, we propose Entropic Control for Homeostatic Optimization (ECHO), a closed-loop control framework. By decomposing the KL divergence, we identify output entropy as a dominant observable component of KL variation. This enables us to leverage entropy as a computationally efficient online proxy to monitor forgetting risks in real-time, bypassing expensive reference-model inference. Consequently, ECHO employs an elastic controller that dynamically modulates the gradient weight of replay data via a proportional control law, using deviations from the pre-trained entropic equilibrium as an error signal. Empirical evaluations across 0.6B to 9B parameter architectures demonstrate that ECHO lies on, and in several comparisons extends, the observed plasticity-stability frontier and maintains high operational robustness against varying data mixing ratios.
authors: Shangxi Wu, Xiaorong Yan, Xiaojun Meng, Yuxiang Zhang, Jiansheng Wei
bullets: Addresses the plasticity–stability trade-off in supervised fine-tuning of LLMs.
Decomposes KL divergence to identify output entropy as an efficient proxy for monitoring forgetting risk.
Uses a proportional controller to adjust the gradient weight of replay data based on deviations from pretrained entropic equilibrium.
Evaluations across 0.6B–9B models place ECHO on, and sometimes beyond, the observed plasticity–stability frontier.
Shows robustness across varying data-mixing ratios.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a closed-loop control method to mitigate catastrophic forgetting during LLM fine-tuning, directly relevant to continual/online learning.
papers.title: Entropic Control for Homeostatic Optimization: Pre-empting Catastrophic Forgetting via Dynamic Feedback
papers.tldr: ECHO uses output entropy as a real-time feedback signal to dynamically adjust replay during fine-tuning, reducing catastrophic forgetting without requiring reference-model inference.

papers.abstract: Long-sequence models must retain earlier information. Full attention keeps all past tokens but grows expensive, and recurrent-memory models compress history into fixed slots for linear-time processing. Limited capacity makes writes consequential: distractors can interfere with useful content, while skipped evidence cannot be recalled. Existing multi-slot memories write every token to the same number of slots, merging whether to store it with how many slots to update. We introduce Factorized Write Routing (FWR), which first keeps or skips each token and then chooses a fixed or token-adaptive number of slots. Queries still read all slots. Across ten seeds on two synthetic tasks that query facts after long contexts, we observe a density-dependent reversal. With four slots per write, long-context accuracy favors always writing on dense Feature Recall (0.472 vs 0.337), but learned selective writing on sparse-fact Passkey (0.222 vs 0.048). The tested adaptive rule underperforms fixed allocation under the learned gate on both tasks. A diagnostic oracle given fact labels unavailable at deployment reaches 0.372 on Passkey, showing headroom in filtering distractors. The results suggest avoiding missed writes in information-dense contexts and filtering distractors when they dominate.
authors: Chen Chen, Rui Cheng
bullets: Recurrent memories compress long histories into fixed slots, making write decisions critical: distractors cause interference and skipped evidence is unrecoverable.
Factorized Write Routing (FWR) first decides whether to keep or skip each token, then selects a fixed or token-adaptive number of slots to update.
Across two synthetic long-context tasks and ten seeds, always writing outperformed selective writing on dense Feature Recall (0.472 vs. 0.337).
Selective writing outperformed always writing on sparse-fact Passkey (0.222 vs. 0.048).
The tested adaptive slot-allocation rule underperformed fixed allocation, while an oracle fact filter showed remaining headroom on Passkey.
papers.selection_reason: Factorized write routing for recurrent memory addresses token selection and slot allocation in long-context memory models.
papers.title: Write What Matters: Disentangling Token Selection from Slot Allocation in Recurrent Memory
papers.tldr: Factorizing token selection from slot allocation reveals that selective writing helps sparse-fact recall, while always writing is better in information-dense contexts.

papers.abstract: Instruction-based image editors built on diffusion transformers run tens of denoising steps. Training-free acceleration either reuses features across steps (step caching) or stops computing the regions an edit leaves untouched (region freezing), and the two have been combined before. We ask how a high speed-up target should be split between them. On Qwen-Image-2.1, freezing does more than remove tokens: it lowers the cost of every step, so the step cache can reach the same overall speed-up with a conservative threshold that keeps its error small. A per-step cost model fitted on development runs predicts held-out latency with a median error of 4.0% and reproduces the speed ceilings of the region methods we re-implemented (2.73$\times$ predicted vs. 2.70$\times$ measured for RegionE). Driving frozen tokens to the model's one-step $x_0$ estimate beats returning them to the reference image on every development sample, and in 90% of measured cases the composed error stays below the sum of the two individual errors. The resulting method, FreezePlan, keeps five full steps and gives the rest of the budget to TaylorSeer. On a pre-registered test split it runs 5.05$\times$ faster end to end at 29.8 dB PSNR to the original output, with no significant drop in a VLM judge score; TaylorSeer at 5.02$\times$ reaches 23.5 dB. The curve extends to 5.99$\times$ at 28.0 dB. Swapping in the region selectors of prior methods under our schedule lowers median PSNR by only 0.5--0.6 dB, which places the gain in the schedule and budget split rather than in the selector.
authors: Baiyan Li, Ganxuan Yang
bullets: Region freezing reduces the cost of every denoising step, allowing step caching to operate in a lower-error regime.
A fitted per-step cost model predicts held-out latency with 4.0% median error and accurately estimates method speed ceilings.
Using the model’s one-step x₀ estimate for frozen tokens outperforms restoring the reference image across development samples.
FreezePlan keeps five full steps and allocates the remaining computation budget to TaylorSeer.
On a preregistered test split, it achieves 5.05× end-to-end speedup at 29.8 dB PSNR with no significant VLM-judge score drop; it reaches 5.99× at 28.0 dB.
papers.selection_reason: Training-free acceleration for diffusion image editing via region freezing and step caching; directly reduces compute by pruning spatial tokens and reusing features.
papers.title: Freeze What Is Settled, Cache What Is Smooth: Spatial Freezing Keeps Step Caching in Its Low-Error Regime
papers.tldr: FreezePlan combines spatial region freezing with conservative step caching to achieve 5.05× faster diffusion image editing while preserving output quality.

papers.abstract: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel at zero-shot reasoning, their spatial capabilities are primarily evaluated through static, passive observation. In complex, human-centric scenes, occlusion often hides crucial geometric evidence, and passive benchmarks force models to guess rather than recognize their own visual uncertainty. To bridge this gap, we introduce SATE-Bench, a novel interactive benchmark comprising 316 real-world scenes and 2,525 multi-turn QA pairs to evaluate visual self-awareness and active exocentric view-exploration. It combines a Passive multi-view control with an Active exploration setting, where models start from a severely occluded view and must iteratively query adjacent viewpoints until they gather enough evidence to fully ``sate'' the question, scored by a step-penalized efficiency reward. Evaluating state-of-the-art MLLMs reveals that they terminate exploration prematurely while reporting high confidence, and struggle with fine-grained 3D geometric tasks; matched-view controls further attribute the Active--Passive gap primarily to insufficient evidence acquisition. Moreover, fine-tuning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) shows that rewarding view-seeking increases active exploration but lowers overall accuracy, as models over-explore and fail to fuse expanding multi-view contexts across turns. These findings indicate that scaling passive multi-view perception does not intrinsically yield active spatial reasoning, highlighting the need for models that know where to look, how to integrate what they see, and when to stop. Code and data are available at https://gtc-gh.github.io/SATE-Bench/
authors: Tianchen Guo, Tengyue Zhang, Chen Liu, Ling Chen, Xin Yu
bullets: Introduces an interactive benchmark with real-world scenes and multi-turn questions, covering passive multi-view control and active exocentric exploration.
Models must query adjacent viewpoints from severely occluded views and are scored on answer quality and exploration efficiency.
State-of-the-art MLLMs often stop too early with high confidence and struggle with fine-grained 3D geometry.
Matched-view comparisons suggest the active–passive performance gap mainly stems from insufficient evidence acquisition.
GRPO-based view-seeking increases exploration but can reduce accuracy because models over-explore and fail to integrate views across turns.
papers.selection_reason: Interactive benchmark for MLLM human-centric spatial understanding and active view exploration, directly fitting spatial intelligence.
papers.title: Humans in Space: Can MLLMs Construct Human-Centric Spatial Understanding via Active Exocentric Exploration?
papers.tldr: SATE-Bench evaluates whether MLLMs can actively seek informative viewpoints and build reliable human-centric spatial understanding in occluded scenes.

papers.abstract: Long-context language models can increasingly process entire documents, making full-context prompting a practical alternative to passage retrieval. However, greater capacity determines how much information a model can receive, but not which information best supports a query. This distinction motivates rethinking retrieval: when the full document already fits, can selecting and organizing its evidence improve answering? The challenge is to retain supporting facts and relations while keeping the context focused on the question. To reconcile these goals, we introduce \ours, a training-free framework that uses semantic abstraction to guide selection while retaining original text for answering. \ours constructs a reusable semantic hierarchy from the full document in a single generation, linking node descriptions to source spans. Given a query, structural--semantic scoring and fine-grained lexical attribution nominate shared source nodes; their union with ancestor context preserves structural relations and complete local text. Across four frontier answer models, \ours improves average QA-F1 by 1.72 points over full-context prompting on three LongBench tasks, surpassing the evaluated baselines on the four-model average while reducing answer-context length by 58.55\%. Our code is available at the $\href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/treefuse-ECFE}{repository}$.
authors: Zhe Xu, Tianhao Liao, Zhenqing Ling, Ying Shen, Yaliang Li, Daoyuan Chen
bullets: Addresses the limitation that long-context models can fit entire documents but still need help identifying query-relevant information.
Builds a reusable semantic hierarchy once, linking abstract node descriptions to original source spans.
Uses structural-semantic scoring and fine-grained lexical attribution to select evidence while preserving ancestor context and local text.
Across four answer models and three LongBench tasks, improves average QA-F1 by 1.72 points over full-context prompting.
Reduces answer-context length by 58.55% and surpasses evaluated baselines on the four-model average.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a training-free framework using semantic trees to guide adaptive context construction, improving long-context QA performance.
papers.title: Rethinking Retrieval in the Long-Context Era: Training-Free Semantic Trees for Adaptive Context Construction
papers.tldr: A training-free semantic-tree framework selects and organizes the most relevant evidence from full documents, improving long-context QA while substantially shortening answer contexts.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning adapts pretrained models to new tasks, but identifying which weight changes support the resulting behavior remains difficult. Weight-space interpretability assigns semantic descriptions to these changes, called fine-tuning deltas. Such descriptions leave open how much task performance depends on the identified updates, particularly when other updates can support the same predictions. We address this gap by pairing reversion, which restores selected parameters to their pretrained values, with retention, which keeps only selected fine-tuning updates. We evaluate Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) models on synthetic financial charts, Flowers102, EuroSAT, and FGVCAircraft with ViT-L/14, and on Flowers102 with ViT-B/16, using a shared recipe that tunes the final six visual blocks. Our contributions are threefold. First, attention value-output (VO) updates alone recover 43-87% of the accuracy improvement, although reverting them leaves chart accuracy unchanged. Cross-entropy loss preserves this contrast on Charts and EuroSAT, while correct-class score margins reveal additional contributions. Second, VO weights recover more loss improvement than all ten equally sized, layer-matched random subsets in each setting. VO and multilayer perceptron (MLP) retentions jointly correct 25-81% of pretrained errors, demonstrating overlapping recovered behavior, which we call operational redundancy. Third, removing semantically selected directions reduces VO-retained recovery more than matched-random removal in all five settings. Together, these results distinguish semantic alignment, removal cost, and retained recovery as complementary evidence about the functional role of fine-tuning updates within the evaluated CLIP recipe.
authors: Chih-Ting Liao, Kezhen Bao, Xin Cao
bullets: Fine-tuned CLIP models are evaluated on synthetic financial charts, Flowers102, EuroSAT, and FGVCAircraft using ViT-L/14, plus Flowers102 with ViT-B/16.
Attention value-output (VO) updates alone recover 43–87% of the accuracy improvement, though reverting them does not change chart accuracy.
VO updates recover more loss improvement than matched random subsets across all evaluated settings.
VO and MLP retentions jointly correct 25–81% of pretrained errors, indicating operational redundancy in recovered behavior.
Removing semantically selected directions harms VO-retained recovery more than matched-random removal in all five settings.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes functional content in CLIP fine-tuning deltas, relevant to understanding multimodal foundation model behavior.
papers.title: Reversion, Retention, and Semantic Intervention: Measuring Functional Content in CLIP Fine-Tuning Deltas
papers.tldr: The study uses reversion and retention tests to measure which semantically identified CLIP fine-tuning updates functionally support task adaptation, revealing substantial but overlapping roles for attention VO and MLP updates.

papers.abstract: Indoor IoT cameras can support assisted living and activity-aware spaces, but exporting raw RGB frames raises privacy concerns by exposing facial, clothing, and household details that body-motion tasks often do not require. We present StickFigure, a pose-only IoT camera system that, during real-time monitoring, keeps raw frames local and ephemeral while exporting only compact skeleton streams sufficient for downstream human activity recognition (HAR). While pose estimation has matured on GPUs, extracting accurate pose streams on resource-constrained IoT cameras remains difficult. To overcome these challenges and enable on-device pose streams on (almost) any IoT camera, we present two core designs in StickFigure: an activation-aware pose backbone that allocates channel capacity after spatial downsampling and a lightweight hierarchical MLP refiner that selectively corrects elbow and wrist coordinates using intermediate visual features and kinematic context. We fully implement StickFigure and evaluate it on public benchmarks and real-world deployment. Compared with state-of-the-art MCU pose models, StickFigure achieves the highest pose accuracy and downstream HAR utility on both NTU RGB+D and Penn Action, while using 96.5% fewer parameters and 99.3% fewer MACs per frame than RTMPose-S-based baselines, achieving 0.107 s p95 latency on a representative STM32H753 MCU. We believe StickFigure establishes a new operating point for privacy-aware edge vision on massive IoT cameras.
authors: Aveline Xiaoyuan Han, Chenshu Wu
bullets: Keeps raw RGB frames local and ephemeral, reducing exposure of facial, clothing, and household details.
Uses an activation-aware pose backbone and a lightweight hierarchical MLP refiner for accurate on-device pose estimation.
Improves elbow and wrist coordinates using visual features and kinematic context.
Achieves strong pose accuracy and downstream HAR utility on NTU RGB+D and Penn Action benchmarks.
Runs with 96.5% fewer parameters, 99.3% fewer MACs, and 0.107 s p95 latency on an STM32H753 MCU versus RTMPose-S-based baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Pose-only edge vision system with drastically reduced parameters and MACs, fitting efficient AI broadly.
papers.title: StickFigure: Enabling Pose-Only IoT Cameras for Privacy-Preserving Edge Vision
papers.tldr: StickFigure enables privacy-preserving human activity recognition by processing pose locally on IoT cameras and exporting only compact skeleton streams.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map a language instruction and the current observation directly to actions, without checking whether the instruction has been completed. For long-horizon tasks, a single failed step therefore goes unnoticed and leaves the whole task unfinished. Such failed episodes, however, often end with the task partially complete. Moreover, the unfinished steps are reusable atomic skills that recur across demonstrations. A failed attempt can thus be recovered by composing with atomic skills. We propose RoboDuo, a closed-loop dual-system framework that uses code as the interface between a coding agent and two VLAs. The agent writes a program that lets a full-task VLA attempt the whole task and checks whether it is complete; on failure, an atomic VLA finishes the remaining steps. Since the agent emits no actions and only decides which VLA for execution, RoboDuo wraps an existing full-task VLA without updating its weights. To train the atomic VLA and the coding agent with the completion-checking ability, we build LIBERO-Atomic, LIBERO-Code, and LIBERO-Judge from a single set of LIBERO demonstrations. RoboDuo consistently improves X-VLA and $\pi_{0.5}$ on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, with the largest gains on long-horizon tasks, and recovers failed rollouts of a frozen full-task VLA on a real robot.
authors: Jie Wang, Bo Zhang, Renzhi Lu, Jianyu Chen
bullets: Addresses unnoticed failures in VLAs that can leave long-horizon tasks incomplete.
Uses code to coordinate a full-task VLA, a completion checker, and an atomic-skill VLA in a closed loop.
The coding agent selects which VLA executes actions and does not require updating the full-task VLA’s weights.
Introduces LIBERO-Atomic, LIBERO-Code, and LIBERO-Judge, built from existing LIBERO demonstrations.
Improves X-VLA and π₀.₅ on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, especially for long-horizon tasks, and recovers failures on a real robot.
papers.selection_reason: Closed-loop VLA recovery via code-based atomic skills directly fits vision-language-action and robot learning/manipulation.
papers.title: RoboDuo: Attempt, Check and Atomic Recovery through Code for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: RoboDuo improves long-horizon VLA task completion by checking full-task attempts and recovering failures with reusable atomic skills.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding significantly accelerates autoregressive text generation in Large Language Models (LLMs), but its efficacy depends largely on two key factors: the distributional alignment between the draft and the target model, and the draft model's latency during inference. However, existing approaches typically utilize independently pretrained small draft models or seek to prune the target model to a manually chosen architecture, thereby failing to explicitly balance the trade-off between draft model alignment and token generation efficiency. To address this gap, we formulate draft model design as an optimization problem and propose T2D, a framework that constructs draft models directly from the target model using latency-aware structured pruning and knowledge distillation. In this manner, T2D obtains draft models that are jointly optimized for both measured inference latency and cross-entropy loss on the target model's responses, resulting in superlative speculative decoding performance. Through extensive experiments on multi-domain speculative decoding benchmarks and across several target model families of differing scale, we demonstrate how T2D prunes up to 92\% of the target model to obtain highly performant draft models compared to competitive baselines. Moreover, draft models obtained via T2D can also be utilized by other speculative decoding token-alignment and knowledge distillation methods in a plug-and-play fashion, leading to further gains. Our findings underscore the importance of jointly navigating the draft model architecture-alignment frontier to unlock the full potential of speculative decoding for LLMs.
authors: Shahriar Kabir Nahin, Xiao Ye, Muhao Chen, Ben Zhou, Anshuman Chhabra
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between draft-model inference latency and distributional alignment with the target model.
Uses latency-aware structured pruning plus knowledge distillation to formulate draft-model design as an optimization problem.
Prunes up to 92% of the target model while maintaining strong speculative decoding performance across multiple domains and target-model scales.
The resulting draft models can plug into other token-alignment and distillation methods for additional gains.
Scope: effectiveness depends on measured latency and cross-entropy alignment with the target model’s responses.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes T2D, a framework for pruning and adapting draft models to optimize speculative decoding efficiency and alignment simultaneously.
papers.title: T2D: Target-to-Draft Model Pruning & Adaptation for Efficient Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: T2D builds latency-efficient draft models directly from a target LLM by jointly optimizing structural pruning and target-model alignment for speculative decoding.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D occupancy prediction is important for embodied agents operating in complex environments whose semantic categories extend beyond fixed taxonomies. While recent studies have explored open-vocabulary occupancy in outdoor driving scenarios, indoor environments remain challenging due to dense occlusions, complex geometry, and fine-grained long-tailed semantics. To reduce the need for expensive voxel-level semantic annotations, we study a geometry-only supervision setting requiring only binary occupancy labels. We build upon Language-Embedded Gaussians as a unified representation coupling 3D geometry with language-aligned semantics. For geometry learning, we introduce an opacity-aware Poisson-based Gaussian-to-Occupancy formulation that enables stable volumetric aggregation under binary occupancy supervision. For semantic learning, we render Gaussian features into images and align them with a frozen open-vocabulary model, together with Progressive Temperature Decay to reduce feature mixing during Gaussian splatting. Building on this framework, we further introduce Instance-Level Semantic Consistency to alleviate fragmented object predictions, and Covisibility-Aware Support-View Selection to provide informative and less redundant multi-view semantic supervision. We also extend our framework to outdoor driving scenarios to evaluate its generality across substantially different environments. Extensive experiments on indoor and outdoor benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves strong open-vocabulary occupancy performance, validating the effectiveness and generality of our framework. Code will be available at https://github.com/JuIvyy/LegoOcc.
authors: Changqing Zhou, Yueru Luo, Han Zhang, Zeyu Jiang, Changhao Chen
bullets: Targets indoor and outdoor scenes with dense occlusions, complex geometry, and long-tailed semantics beyond fixed taxonomies.
Uses binary occupancy labels for geometry, with an opacity-aware Poisson Gaussian-to-occupancy formulation for stable volumetric aggregation.
Aligns rendered Gaussian features with a frozen open-vocabulary model and applies Progressive Temperature Decay to reduce feature mixing.
Introduces Instance-Level Semantic Consistency and Covisibility-Aware Support-View Selection to improve fragmented and redundant multi-view predictions.
Experiments on indoor and outdoor benchmarks show strong performance and cross-environment generality.
papers.selection_reason: Open-vocabulary 3D occupancy prediction couples geometry with language-aligned semantics, fitting 3D perception and spatial understanding.
papers.title: LegoOcc++: Towards Consistent Open-Vocabulary 3D Occupancy Prediction
papers.tldr: LegoOcc++ enables open-vocabulary 3D occupancy prediction from geometry-only supervision by combining language-aligned Gaussian representations with consistency-aware semantic learning.

papers.abstract: Few-step distillation for autoregressive (AR) video generation commonly first initializes an AR student and then refines it with distribution matching distillation (DMD). This refinement process faces two challenges. First, although initialization already yields a reasonably capable student, DMD obtains the refinement direction indirectly by estimating the full student score before forming the teacher-student correction. Second, detached-history training prevents the generator from assigning credit to a current chunk for its influence on subsequent chunks. We introduce Leta, a few-step distillation framework that addresses these challenges with ScoreDelta and FutureCredit. ScoreDelta directly estimates the teacher-student correction from denoising residuals, while FutureCredit learns an auxiliary cross-chunk update signal from vector-Jacobian products (VJPs) of next-chunk teacher residuals. Leta combines these signals into a joint teacher-guided update field in a single forward pass during generator updates. Teacher evaluations and credit VJPs are used only for estimator training. For ScoreDelta, we establish population equivalence to score-difference estimation and a conditional approximation advantage under limited capacity in a fixed-feature linear model. In our controlled experiments, Leta improves over DMD by 0.9 points on VBench and 0.66 on VideoAlign. This advantage persists at a higher generator update frequency (a generator-to-estimator update ratio of G:E=1:1), where Leta improves over DMD by 1.6 on VBench and 0.35 on VideoAlign. Project page: https://scdzx.github.io/Leta/.
authors: Zixuan Duan, Yabo Chen, Xunzhi Xiang, Xin Zhang, Haibin Huang, Yin Chen, Chi Zhang, Qi Fan
bullets: Addresses two DMD limitations: indirect score estimation and detached-history training.
ScoreDelta estimates the teacher–student correction directly from denoising residuals.
FutureCredit learns cross-chunk credit using vector-Jacobian products of next-chunk teacher residuals.
Combines both signals into a joint teacher-guided update field in one generator-update forward pass.
Controlled experiments report gains over DMD on VBench and VideoAlign, including at a 1:1 generator-to-estimator update ratio.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a distillation framework for autoregressive video generation, directly relevant to autoregressive video models.
papers.title: Learning the Autoregressive: Direct Score-Difference Estimation with Amortized Future Credit for Video Distillation
papers.tldr: Leta improves few-step autoregressive video distillation by directly estimating teacher–student score differences and crediting earlier chunks for their future impact.

papers.abstract: We introduce the Literature and Linguistics Analysis Benchmark (LALA), comprising 236 open-ended questions written by experts in linguistics and literary studies, together with expert-provided ideal answers. By comparing models within families and at similar training scales using human and LLM judges, LALA identifies differences in linguistic competence associated with post-training, offering a framework for evaluating future models and guiding targeted improvements. We administered questions to 17 language models and evaluated their responses using both human expert assessment and two LLM evaluators, Sol and Qwen. Base models displayed little of the linguistic competence assessed by the benchmark, whereas their post-trained versions performed markedly better, suggesting that post-training plays a central role in making linguistic knowledge accessible and usable. Parameter count, by contrast, showed no statistically significant association with partial-credit performance, and competencies remained unevenly distributed across linguistic domains. We interpret this pattern as evidence that post-training adds linguistic competencies piecemeal, without producing a general linguistic intelligence capable of extending them beyond the learned policies that support them. Models performed best on logical relations between statements and selected discourse-level tasks, while even the strongest post-trained models continued to struggle with ambiguity, literary style, reference, and misleading assumptions. Human and Sol evaluations produced nearly identical model rankings in both the original and ReliableEval runs, supporting the replicability of the comparative results.
authors: Michael Foster, Barbara McGillivray, Gard B. Jenset, Jakub M\'acha, Jason Harding, Marcus Perlman, Devyani Sharma, Patrick Skeels, Jana Willer-Gold, Jeannette Littlemore
bullets: Introduces 236 expert-written open-ended questions with ideal answers spanning linguistics and literary studies.
Evaluates 17 models using human experts and two LLM judges, with largely consistent comparative rankings.
Post-trained models outperform base models, while parameter count has no significant association with partial-credit performance.
Models perform best on logical relations and some discourse tasks, but struggle with ambiguity, literary style, reference, and misleading assumptions.
Results suggest post-training adds competencies piecemeal rather than creating general linguistic intelligence beyond learned policies.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces the LALA benchmark for evaluating literary and linguistic analysis capabilities in LLMs, offering a framework for assessing post-training effects.
papers.title: The LALA Benchmark: Evaluating Literary and Linguistic Analysis in LLMs
papers.tldr: LALA evaluates LLMs’ literary and linguistic reasoning, finding that post-training substantially improves access to linguistic competence, while abilities remain uneven and limited in scope.

papers.abstract: Jailbreak benchmarks test one checkpoint and treat which jailbreaks break it as a property of its pretraining data and safety training. We ask whether another pretraining run of the same data, given the same safety training, would break on the same jailbreaks. For each of 25 pretraining data recipes, we take 1B base models from 3 pretraining seeds and give each the same safety post-training with 2 post-training seeds, for 150 models in all. We then collect 20 responses from every model to a shared set of jailbreak prompts and correlate the per-prompt non-refusal rates between every pair of models. On average, two post-trained copies of the same pretraining run have per-prompt non-refusal rates that correlate at 0.984. A different pretraining seed lowers the correlation to 0.811, and a different data recipe lowers it only slightly further, to 0.779. These results indicate that which jailbreaks break a checkpoint depends much more on its pretraining run than on its data, a pattern that holds in all 25 data recipes and at 150M and 300M parameters. In practice, the best of 91 attack templates found on one checkpoint stays the best after a new pretraining seed in only 27% of model pairs, against 67% after a new post-training seed. Each pretraining run also leaves a fingerprint: across 3,211 prompts, a model's per-prompt non-refusal rates identify its pretraining run among all 75 runs every time, and a random subset of 50 prompts still does so 98% of the time.
authors: Chi-Wei Chang, Mu-Tien Kuo, Kuan-Wei Lee, Meng-Hsun Tsai
bullets: The study evaluates 150 models from 25 data recipes, 3 pretraining seeds, and 2 post-training seeds using shared jailbreak prompts.
Same-pretraining-run copies have highly similar per-prompt non-refusal patterns (correlation 0.984), while changing the pretraining seed drops correlation to 0.811.
Changing the data recipe lowers correlation only slightly further, to 0.779; the pattern also holds at 150M and 300M parameters.
The best attack template transfers across pretraining seeds only 27% of the time, versus 67% across post-training seeds.
Per-prompt non-refusal behavior fingerprints the pretraining run: identification succeeds every time across 3,211 prompts and 98% of the time using 50 prompts.
papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates that pretraining runs leave unique fingerprints affecting jailbreak susceptibility, providing insights into LLM robustness and data composition.
papers.title: Identically Trained Language Models Break on Different Jailbreaks
papers.tldr: Which jailbreaks succeed depends far more on a model’s specific pretraining run than on its data recipe or safety-training seed.

papers.abstract: Memory is increasingly used in long-horizon agents, yet the net value of building memory over direct retrieval from raw history remains largely unclear. Through a large-scale evaluation across multiple benchmarks and model backbones, we find many dedicated memory systems underperform naive RAG in many cases, indicating a negative net value. Taking RAG as a reference, we dissect the net value of memory into the gains and losses over direct retrieval, termed memory benefit and memory tax. These gains and losses arise because memory process changes how the raw information is organized and accessed. We view such changes as the double-edged deviations from the raw history. They are originally designed and introduced to benefit the task, for example by reorganizing facts or distilling preferences, but some may also remove or obscure evidence, giving rise to memory tax. Since memory benefit reflects the expected gains of its design, we then focus more on the overlooked memory tax, study how it arises from the system and evaluation side, and generalize the concept to more application scenarios of memory. We hope the notion of memory tax can provide a new lens and shift more attention from standalone performance to the net value of memory, informing more reliable memory designs and evaluations. We will open-source the code and results to the community. Project Page: https://hexuan21.github.io/MemoryTax/
authors: Xuan He, Sining Zhoubian, Ruozhen Yang, Yuhao Wen, Zhineng Wang, Yuyang Hu, Ke Yang, Yuyu Zhang, Ping Nie, Jiawei Han, ChengXiang Zhai
bullets: Evaluates memory systems across multiple benchmarks and model backbones against naive RAG.
Defines memory benefit as gains over direct retrieval and memory tax as corresponding losses.
Attributes both effects to how memory reorganizes, distills, or obscures raw information.
Studies how memory tax arises from system and evaluation factors and extends the concept to broader memory applications.
Advocates evaluating the net value and reliability of memory rather than standalone performance; code and results will be released.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces the concept of 'Memory Tax' to dissect the net value of memory systems in long-horizon agents, contrasting them with direct retrieval.
papers.title: Memory Tax: Dissecting the Net Value of Agent Memory
papers.tldr: Dedicated agent memory can hurt performance relative to retrieving directly from raw history, so its value should be measured as benefits minus memory-induced losses.

papers.abstract: Robot tasks require grounding spatial language in physical scenes, but task success alone cannot establish whether spatial instructions are followed. We present BEHAVIOR-Spatial, a benchmark built on BEHAVIOR-1K that measures spatial question answering, point-based target grounding, and robot action to examine how VLM spatial understanding relates to VLA behavior. It comprises 3,256 spatial questions across 49 activities, 1,240 grounding queries across 14 manipulation tasks, and action evaluations covering those 14 tasks and 10 navigation tasks. Our manipulation protocol evaluates held-out configurations and instruction following when the requested target changes within a fixed training layout. The baseline achieves 41.6% on held-out configurations but only 16.1% under changed instructions. VLM adaptation and robot-data pretraining provide limited improvements, whereas oracle visual target cues raise these rates to 60.3% and 38.0%, respectively. Perception evaluations reveal policy-dependent correlations between VLM question-answering and grounding accuracy and VLA manipulation performance. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial instruction following alongside task completion and examining when spatial perception performance translates into robot behavior. Project website: https://arielchen07.github.io/behavior-spatial/.
authors: Sirui Chen, Huang Huang, Qineng Wang, Wenlong Huang, Manling Li, Ruohan Zhang, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu
bullets: Benchmarks spatial question answering, point-based target grounding, and robot actions on BEHAVIOR-1K.
Includes 3,256 spatial questions, 1,240 grounding queries, 14 manipulation tasks, and 10 navigation tasks.
Tests held-out scene configurations and target changes under fixed training layouts.
Baseline action success drops from 41.6% on held-out configurations to 16.1% with changed instructions; oracle visual cues improve both settings.
Shows that perception accuracy does not consistently translate into robot behavior, motivating joint evaluation of spatial understanding and task completion.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark linking VLM spatial understanding to VLA behavior in manipulation and navigation; fits spatial intelligence and embodied robotics.
papers.title: Behavior Spatial Benchmark: Evaluating Spatial Understanding for Robotics
papers.tldr: BEHAVIOR-Spatial evaluates whether vision-language models and robot policies truly understand and follow spatial instructions in physical scenes.

papers.abstract: LVLM benchmarks tell us whether a model answers correctly, but not which visual conventions it has retained, nor where those conventions live. Sketches expose this hidden structure. A sketch removes texture, lighting, and photographic context while preserving the strokes humans judged sufficient for recognition. If an LVLM can operate on that abstraction, the surviving signal is structural rather than merely photometric. We introduce a training-free sketch probe with three readouts: temporal part-construction order, spatial attention-based grounding, and the mechanistic layer/head locus of grounding. We evaluate nine LVLMs on part order and five on the attention readouts, over two part-annotated sketch datasets. Three findings emerge. First, LVLM part order tracks human convention: models reproduce canonical orderings where human drawings converge, and become correspondingly variable where human orderings vary. Controls that blank, withhold, and mismatch the sketch locate this convention in the language model. Second, part-level grounding survives the abstraction: attention heads selected from the frozen model with an existing recipe recover part and object regions on object and scene sketches, with no grounding supervision. Third, the grounding signal concentrates in a narrow mid-network band whose location follows the base language model rather than parameter count in the two families we compare, and remains stable across object and scene sketches. The result is a practical diagnostic for sketch-driven LVLMs: no fine-tuning, no auxiliary segmenter, and a layer band that doubles as a head-selection prior, matching or improving grounding mAcc@0.1 in every model and dataset we tested.
authors: Chaitat Utintu, Ahmed Bourouis, Arkaprabha Basu, Yi-Zhe Song
bullets: Introduces a training-free sketch probe measuring temporal part order, spatial grounding, and the mechanistic layer/head location of grounding.
Across nine LVLMs, part-construction order follows human conventions: canonical where people agree and variable where human order varies.
Across five LVLMs, attention-based grounding recovers object and part regions from object and scene sketches without grounding supervision.
Grounding concentrates in a stable mid-network layer band tied to the base language model rather than parameter count in the studied families.
The probe matches or improves grounding mAcc@0.1 in every tested model and dataset, without fine-tuning or an auxiliary segmenter.
papers.selection_reason: Probes LVLM visual conventions, grounding, and localization, contributing to multimodal foundation model analysis.
papers.title: What Sketches Tell Us about LVLMs: Conventions, Grounding, and Localisation
papers.tldr: Sketches reveal that LVLMs retain human-like visual conventions and part-level grounding, with grounding concentrated in a narrow, language-model-dependent mid-network band.

papers.abstract: Camera motion recognition requires separating viewpoint changes caused by camera translation, rotation, or zoom from object motion and scene dynamics. Video-language models often rely on semantic cues and struggle with the geometric evidence needed for this task. Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures such as V-JEPA offer strong spatio-temporal representations, but our experiments suggest that they underrepresent geometric cues in some regions. Under temporal-reversal supervision, V-JEPA improves overall but degrades on several motion families, whereas a weaker geometry-oriented VGGT predictor improves across all families. We refer to these geometrically underrepresented regions as geometric blind spots and propose Fovea-JEPA to identify and address them. Using V-JEPA as the base model and VGGT as a geometry expert, we construct intervention pseudo-labels from their prediction errors to weakly supervise a blind-spot predictor. The predictor produces token-wise response maps, which are aggregated into a clip-level intervention score to guide adaptive fusion of visual and geometric features. This selective intervention introduces complementary geometric information while preserving reliable visual predictions. Experiments on CameraMotionDataset, CameraBench, and ShotBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Fovea-JEPA, with gains of 9.67, 8.67, and 24.38 percentage points over previously reported state-of-the-art baselines, respectively. Code and models will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Xiangkun Shi, Hanhui Li, Shiyue Zhang, Chang Liu, Junwen Pan, Zhenbang Sun, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Targets geometric blind spots in video representations that hinder distinguishing camera motion from object and scene dynamics.
Uses V-JEPA as the base model and VGGT as a geometry expert to create error-based pseudo-labels for blind-spot supervision.
Aggregates token-level blind-spot responses into clip-level scores that guide adaptive fusion of visual and geometric features.
Reports gains of 9.67, 8.67, and 24.38 percentage points over prior state-of-the-art baselines on CameraMotionDataset, CameraBench, and ShotBench.
Scope: addresses camera-motion recognition through selective geometric intervention while preserving reliable visual predictions.
papers.selection_reason: Improves video-language models for camera motion recognition via geometric blind-spot intervention, fitting video understanding.
papers.title: Fovea-JEPA: Overcoming Geometric Blind Spots in V-JEPA for Camera Motion Recognition
papers.tldr: Fovea-JEPA improves camera-motion recognition by detecting where V-JEPA misses geometric cues and selectively injecting information from a geometry-focused predictor.

papers.abstract: Robots that learn from people often see several valid ways to do the same task: pass an obstacle on the left or on the right, open the microwave or move the kettle first. A policy that re-decides at every step can waver between these ways mid-task. We ask when the action head (the part of a policy that turns the state into actions) matters, and how it should make this choice. On a controlled task, heads that sample one way succeed far more often than a head that averages the ways when the demonstrations contain several ways and the state gives no hint which to take (+0.72 success with two ways); this trend was not reproduced on the other tasks we ran. We then present ElevateHead, a head that decides once at a learned decision point, commits to that choice for the episode, and exposes the choice as an input a user can set. We designed it by diagnosis: each version was frozen and tested on tasks it had not seen, and the next version changed only what a measured failure pointed to; predictions were registered before each run. The first four versions each fell below BeT on at least one held-out task. The fifth completed all four subtasks of the held-out Franka Kitchen task in 45.2% of episodes against 29.3% for BeT, the strongest baseline across our tasks (+0.160, 95% CI [+0.129, +0.188]); when a mode was forced, the first completed subtask matched it in 95% of successful episodes. Diagnosis also located where commitment breaks: varied start positions (repaired on the controlled task: commitment 0.22 to 0.81, success 0.74 to 0.91) and varied object placement (partly repaired: in an exploratory variant, commitment 0.03 to 0.59 on aligning with no detectable change in success). On held-out block stacking, version 4 was comparable to BeT and did not exceed it. A real-robot test with predictions fixed in advance is planned for a follow-up version of this paper.
authors: Tsung-Lung Yang
bullets: Per-step averaging can fail when demonstrations contain multiple valid strategies and observations do not reveal which strategy to choose; sampling performed better on one controlled task, but this trend did not generalize to all tasks.
ElevateHead selects a mode once, commits to it, and lets users set the selected mode explicitly.
Through iterative diagnosis on unseen tasks, the fifth version achieved 45.2% success on all four Franka Kitchen subtasks versus 29.3% for BeT.
Forced modes matched the first completed subtask in 95% of successful episodes, supporting controllable behavior.
Commitment was sensitive to varied starts and object placements; performance was comparable to BeT on held-out block stacking, and real-robot evaluation remains future work.
papers.selection_reason: Action head design for multimodal imitation learning in robot manipulation.
papers.title: ElevateHead: Decide Once, Then Commit: When the Action Head Matters for Multimodal Imitation
papers.tldr: ElevateHead improves multimodal imitation by making one interpretable action-mode choice at a learned point and committing to it for the episode.

papers.abstract: As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) increasingly enable robots to follow language instructions, understanding their navigation decisions becomes important for reliable deployment. Existing explainability methods overlook a key challenge in Vision-Language Navigation (VLN): evidence for the current action may be distributed across historical and current observations and associated with different instruction stages. We identify instruction-stage insensitivity, where existing methods produce similar explanations despite changes across different navigation stages. To address this issue, we propose a stage-aware attribution framework for VLN. We first construct action-conditioned temporal instruction--visual attributions across observations. These attributions are projected into instruction space to estimate stage associations, which guide the aggregation of relevant historical evidence for refining the current explanation. An instruction-guided spatial filter further suppresses isolated responses while preserving compact, instruction-relevant regions. Experiments across multiple VLN policies and benchmarks show improved attribution quality over existing methods. We further demonstrate that our method acts as a diagnostic tool for analyzing failure cases, and validate its applicability to real-world navigation on a Unitree G1 robot.
authors: Yiyuan Yao, Xinpeng Ding, Minglei Chen, Fei Gao, Lihuo He, Jie Yuan, Aijun Li, Nannan Wang, Xinbo Gao
bullets: Addresses instruction-stage insensitivity in existing VLN explanations.
Builds action-conditioned temporal instruction–visual attributions across observations.
Projects attributions into instruction space to identify stages and aggregate relevant historical evidence.
Uses an instruction-guided spatial filter to remove isolated responses while preserving compact relevant regions.
Improves attribution quality across multiple policies and benchmarks, supports failure analysis, and transfers to a Unitree G1 robot.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses explainability for Vision-Language Navigation, a core configured subtopic.
papers.title: Explaining Navigation Decisions: Stage-Aware Visual Attribution for Vision-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: A stage-aware attribution framework explains VLN actions by linking instruction stages to relevant visual evidence across current and historical observations.

papers.abstract: GEPA is among the strongest reflective prompt optimizers for language-model programs, but its system-aware merge operator is unstable across models: merge improves gpt-4.1-mini on average while degrading Qwen3-8B, an asymmetry noted but left unexplained by the GEPA paper. We investigate this instability across five datasets and two models. Our nine-configuration sweep over merge timing and merge operator shows that merge can improve both models when configured appropriately. This suggests that merge instability is better explained by configuration sensitivity than by an inherent flaw in the merge operator. We then test whether prompt-level features predict GEPA's merge-accept decisions and find that they do not, ruling out static-feature gating. As a proof of concept, a behavior-based probe built from these diagnostics avoids large merge failures in our multi-seed runs by abstaining on high-risk tasks, although it does not consistently outperform NoMerge. Code is available as GEPA-MergeProbe at https://github.com/ChongZZZZ/GEPA_MERGE .
authors: Chong Zhao, Ruyi Yang, Changming Liu, Alice Zhao
bullets: Studies GEPA merging across five datasets, two models, and nine merge configurations.
Finds appropriate merge timing and operators can improve both gpt-4.1-mini and Qwen3-8B.
Shows static prompt features do not predict merge-accept decisions.
A behavior-based probe avoids large merge failures in multi-seed runs by abstaining on high-risk tasks.
The probe does not consistently outperform NoMerge; code is released as GEPA-MergeProbe.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates the stability of prompt optimizer merge operators and builds a behavior-based diagnostic probe, offering technical insights into LLM optimization.
papers.title: When Does GEPA Merge Help? A Mechanism-Level Diagnostic
papers.tldr: GEPA merge instability appears configuration-sensitive rather than inherent, and behavior-based probing can avoid major failures but does not consistently improve over NoMerge.

papers.abstract: Deep learning facilitates rapid single shot three dimensional (3D) reconstruction using fringe projection profilometry (FPP), but recovering accurate surface height from a single high frequency fringe image remains challenging because both long-range spatial consistency and fine geometric details must be preserved. Convolutional networks are limited in modeling long range dependencies, whereas window-based Transformers establish global interactions only progressively with increasing depth. To address these limitations, a hybrid Mamba Transformer network is proposed for fringe to height regression. The network adopts a Swin based U shaped architecture and introduces visual state space modeling at the intermediate resolution encoder stage. An axial and dilated vision state space (ADVSS) block is further developed to enhance prescan feature encoding through local, dilated, and axial depthwise convolutions while retaining four directional selective scanning. This design combines linear complexity long range modeling with direction aware preservation of local fringe structures. Experiments on a publicly available FPP dataset show that the proposed method outperforms hNet, SwinConvUNet, UHRNet, and HiDNet in mean absolute error(MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), absolute relative error, and structural similarity index measure (SSIM). Using only one deformed fringe image, the proposed method achieves an RMSE of 0.548 mm and an SSIM of 0.9985, reducing RMSE by 65.2% and 59.6% relative to UHRNet and HiDNet, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining selective state space modeling with hierarchical window based attention for accurate single-shot FPP reconstruction.
authors: Xinjie Zhou, XiaoLei Li
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of preserving both global spatial consistency and fine geometric details in single-shot fringe projection profilometry.
Uses a Swin-based U-shaped encoder–decoder with visual state space modeling at an intermediate resolution.
Introduces an axial and dilated vision state space block with local, dilated, and axial convolutions plus four-directional selective scanning.
On a public FPP dataset, outperforms hNet, SwinConvUNet, UHRNet, and HiDNet across MAE, RMSE, absolute relative error, and SSIM.
Achieves 0.548 mm RMSE and 0.9985 SSIM from a single deformed fringe image; evaluation is limited to the reported public dataset and metrics.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a hybrid Mamba-Transformer network for single-shot 3D reconstruction, combining efficient long-range modeling with local detail preservation.
papers.title: Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Network for Single-Shot 3D Reconstruction from Fringe Patterns
papers.tldr: A hybrid Swin Transformer–Mamba network enables accurate single-shot 3D reconstruction from one high-frequency fringe image by combining long-range modeling with fine-detail preservation.

papers.abstract: People have long dreamed of an assistant that is always there to guide them and remind what they forget, from new dishes to lost keys. Powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs), egocentric AI assistants on wearable devices are bringing this dream within reach: they see what the user sees and give instructions for user's physical work when necessary. However, testing such assistance is challenging and usually requires real people. The expensive and rare real interaction data leaves a key question unanswered: Can today's MLLMs truly help people in physical world? To answer this question, we propose InteractiveWorld, the first verifiable environment for closed-loop interaction between human and AI assistant. Unlike existing robot-centric simulators, InteractiveWorld lets the assistant guide a human agent who observes the scene, understands instructions, and acts independently. It thus realistically simulates how AI assistant collaborates with human: the assistant instructs, the human acts, and the environment executes actions and updates what they see next. Building on it, we introduce InteractiveBench, the first dynamic benchmark for egocentric AI assistants, with 120 multi-turn tasks across six categories. In each task, the assistant guides the human in real time, and every instruction shapes the outcome, which is scored by verifiable, state-based rewards. Experiments with 12 frontier MLLMs show they are still far from reliable assistants. Even the strongest model, Claude Fable 5.1, achieves at most 20% and 25% on long-horizon Guidance and Planning tasks, respectively. Overall, our work offers a verifiable platform and a rigorous evaluation set, laying a solid foundation for research on interactive MLLM assistants that truly help people in the physical world.
authors: Qinsi Wang, Wei Wen, Chong Zhou, Saksham Suri, Zechun Liu, Lemeng Wu, Hai Helen Li, Yiran Chen, Raghuraman Krishnamoorthi, Qi Qian
bullets: Addresses the difficulty and cost of evaluating egocentric assistants through real human interaction.
Simulates assistant–human collaboration: the assistant instructs, the human acts, and the environment updates accordingly.
Introduces InteractiveBench with 120 multi-turn tasks spanning six categories and state-based rewards.
Evaluates 12 frontier MLLMs; even the strongest model scores at most 20% on Guidance and 25% on Planning tasks.
Provides a platform and benchmark for developing more capable interactive assistants.
papers.selection_reason: Verifiable human-centric environment for evaluating egocentric interactive MLLM assistants; relevant to embodied multimodal assistants.
