papers.title: InteractiveWorld: A Verifiable Human-Centric Environment for Building Better Interactive MLLM Assistants
papers.tldr: InteractiveWorld enables verifiable, closed-loop evaluation of MLLM assistants guiding humans through physical-world tasks, revealing that current models remain unreliable.

papers.abstract: Automated classification of gastrointestinal (GI) findings in endoscopic images could support early diagnosis, but architectures are often chosen on accuracy alone. We present a controlled, reproducible benchmark of ResNet50 and ViT-B/16 for eight-class GI classification on the public Kvasir dataset (4,000 images), using a stratified split (400 test images) and stratified group 5-fold cross-validation over all images. In cross-validation, ResNet50 and ViT-B/16 reached 92.12% and 91.70% accuracy, and a two one-sided tests (TOST) procedure showed equivalence within a +/-3 percentage-point margin (difference +0.43 points, 90% CI -0.33 to +1.18; p < 0.001). The architectures differed mainly in cost: ResNet50 had 3.6 times fewer parameters and 4.3 times fewer operations, 2.5-fold lower single-image CPU latency (69 vs. 177 ms) and 3.8-fold higher GPU throughput. Cross-validated calibration was similar (expected calibration error 0.021 vs. 0.023). An edge-oriented transformer, MobileViT-S, was most accurate on the test split (95.5%) but lost 9.4 points when an acquisition artefact present in some classes (the ScopeGuide inset) was occluded, whereas ResNet50 was not significantly affected. On 500 unseen polyp images with expert masks, both models' Grad-CAM maps focused on the lesion (3.6 times chance). On a de-duplicated external subset of GastroVision (1,998 images), accuracy fell to 78-80% for all three models and differences between them remained small. Accuracy differences between architectures were thus small relative to the effects of shortcut learning and domain shift, whereas efficiency differences were large. An efficient CNN is a defensible default for resource-constrained screening, but no model is deployment-ready without local validation.
authors: Akwasi Asare
bullets: On Kvasir’s eight-class task, ResNet50 and ViT-B/16 were statistically equivalent within a 3-point accuracy margin.
ResNet50 used fewer parameters and operations, with lower CPU latency and higher GPU throughput than ViT-B/16.
MobileViT-S achieved the highest test-split accuracy but was vulnerable to the ScopeGuide artefact, indicating shortcut learning.
Both ResNet50 and ViT-B/16 showed similar calibration and lesion-focused Grad-CAM explanations.
Accuracy dropped substantially on the external GastroVision subset, highlighting domain-shift risks and the need for local validation.
papers.selection_reason: Provides a benchmark comparing the efficiency (latency, throughput) of ResNet50 and Vision Transformers, highlighting architectural trade-offs for resource-constrained deployment.
papers.title: Accuracy Is Not Enough: An Efficiency- and Statistics-Aware Benchmark of ResNet50 and Vision Transformer for Explainable Multi-Class Gastrointestinal Diseases Classification
papers.tldr: ResNet50 matches ViT-B/16 accuracy for GI disease classification while being substantially more efficient, but shortcut learning and domain shift limit deployment readiness.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation often depends on object properties that cannot be reliably inferred from appearance alone. Physical interaction can reveal these properties, but it can also change the world in ways that invalidate subsequent actions. We present a task and motion planning (TAMP) framework that integrates task-directed interactive information-gathering with interleaved planning and execution. Building on PDDLStream, our framework plans optimistically with these interactive actions, verifies their outcomes during execution, and adapts the remaining plan by retaining still-applicable actions and replanning only the connections needed to continue execution. We evaluate the framework in simulation and on a real robot across tasks that require determining whether an object is movable, a pen has ink, a drawer can be opened, or a container is empty. These experiments demonstrate how interaction-driven state updates and recovery replanning support continued execution under uncertain outcomes and external disturbances.
authors: Linfei Yuan, Rachel Holladay
bullets: Addresses long-horizon manipulation where object properties cannot be determined reliably from appearance.
Integrates task-directed information-gathering actions with interleaved planning and execution.
Plans optimistically, verifies interactive outcomes, and replans only the remaining necessary connections.
Evaluated in simulation and on a real robot across tasks involving movable objects, ink-filled pens, openable drawers, and empty containers.
Supports continued execution despite uncertain interaction outcomes and external disturbances.
papers.selection_reason: TAMP with interactive information gathering for long-horizon manipulation.
papers.title: I Won't Know Until I Try: Interactive Information Gathering for Long-Horizon Manipulation
papers.tldr: A TAMP framework enables robots to gather information through physical interaction while adapting plans when those interactions change the world or produce uncertain outcomes.

papers.abstract: Continual learning is the ability of LLM agents to improve over time by acquiring, refining, and applying knowledge from experience while retaining useful prior knowledge. It is essential for agents learning over long time horizons, yet current evaluations largely assess individual task performance rather than improvement through accumulated experience. We introduce Continual Learning Exam (CLE), a large-scale benchmark developed by 50+ domain experts to measure experience-driven improvement in realistic professional workflows. CLE comprises 120 human-authored tasks, each organised as a five-level ladder, yielding 600 levels spanning 89 professional roles across 12 occupational domains. Agents must pass each level to unlock the next, with later levels building on experience accumulated during earlier assignments. An evaluation agent assesses each submission against human-authored rubrics. We compare a single-submission setting with one that provides diagnostic feedback after failure and allows one revision. Across 17 harness-model configurations using frontier LLMs, feedback and revision yield a median completion gain of 5.3 percentage points. Yet the best-performing system clears only 47.7% of levels and completes all five levels in just 23.3% of tasks, highlighting the difficulty of sustained learning from experience for existing frontier LLMs. As such, the dataset can also be used to post-train LLMs to strengthen their continual learning capabilities.
authors: Haoyu Zhao, Sitian Tu, Yuxuan Huang, Huichi Zhou, Zhangyue Yin, Jiahao Huang, Jingyuan Xu, Tianmiao Shi, Jin Shi, Nianxi Zhang, Yangmiao Zhang, Zhuolang Chan, Huiyan Hu, Chenchao Sheng, Yaqing Luo, Yue Chen, Huaxiu Yao, Meng Fang, Jun Wang
bullets: Introduces 120 expert-authored tasks with five sequential levels each, covering 600 levels, 89 professional roles, and 12 occupational domains.
Agents must pass each level to unlock later levels, testing accumulated experience rather than isolated task performance.
Compares single submissions with diagnostic feedback plus one revision; feedback improves median completion by 5.3 percentage points across 17 configurations.
The strongest system clears 47.7% of levels and completes all five levels for 23.3% of tasks, indicating substantial difficulty with sustained continual learning.
CLE may also support post-training LLMs to improve continual-learning capabilities.
papers.selection_reason: Large-scale benchmark for continual and experiential learning in LLM agents; directly fits continual learning.
papers.title: Continual Learning Exam: Benchmarking Long-Horizon RSI and Experiential Learning in LLM Agents
papers.tldr: CLE benchmarks whether LLM agents can improve through experience and retain performance across long-horizon professional workflows.

papers.abstract: Bimanual robotic control requires simultaneous management of distinct functional demands under motor noise, energetic costs, and communication delays. We investigate how learning responsibility should be organised across modular controllers and the two arms in a simulated musculoskeletal system with two communicating recurrent controllers. Using a 2 x 2 design, we compare differential versus shared controller objectives and fixed versus balanced hand-task assignments. Task-aligned functional specialisation was strongest when differential objectives were combined with a fixed assignment aligned with contralateral control routing. This condition achieved the highest canonical-task performance and control efficiency, reaching 81.33% bimanual success. Its advantage over shared objectives increased with motor noise but narrowed under stronger energy penalties. Stronger specialisation also reduced hand-role flexibility: reversing the hand roles decreased bimanual success by 80.46 percentage points under Differential-Fixed training, compared with 1.51 percentage points under Shared-Balanced training. These results show that controller objectives and hand-task experience jointly determine functional organisation. Stronger role-specific specialisation favours performance and efficiency when roles remain stable, whereas more distributed training favours interchangeability when roles change.
authors: Jingwen Li, Levin Kuhlmann, Jason Friedman, Gideon Kowadlo
bullets: Studies functional specialisation in two communicating recurrent controllers controlling a simulated musculoskeletal bimanual system.
Compares differential versus shared controller objectives and fixed versus balanced hand-task assignments in a 2×2 design.
Differential objectives with fixed, contralaterally aligned assignments produced the strongest specialisation, performance, and control efficiency.
This condition reached 81.33% bimanual success; its advantage increased with motor noise but narrowed under stronger energy penalties.
Specialisation reduced role flexibility: reversing hand roles caused an 80.46-point success drop versus 1.51 points for Shared-Balanced training.
papers.selection_reason: Study of functional specialisation in bimanual robotic control.
papers.title: Learning Functional Specialisation for Bimanual Robotic Control
papers.tldr: Bimanual control improves when controllers specialise for stable, task-aligned hand roles, while distributed training better preserves flexibility when roles change.

papers.abstract: World action models have demonstrated promising performance in robot policy learning, yet their high inference latency remains a critical bottleneck for real-world deployment. Recent approaches have sought to improve inference efficiency by reducing test-time future-frame imagination or accelerating action prediction. However, these methods often leverage representations from all video world model layers without explicitly considering their varying relevance to action prediction, leading to redundant computation and suboptimal representation utilization. In this work, we propose TurboWAM, a fast world action model that efficiently aggregates structured world representations conditioned on action predictions. Specifically, TurboWAM introduces a structured world representation aggregation module that adaptively fuses representations from different world model layers according to their relevance to the evolving action denoising state. Furthermore, TurboWAM employs a structured action supervision mechanism that adaptively modulates gradients from action supervision across different world model layers during backward propagation, facilitating world representation learning. During inference, by reducing the number of world model layers executed and caching relevant representations across action denoising steps, TurboWAM substantially reduces computational overhead. Extensive experiments on multiple robot manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that TurboWAM achieves low inference latency while maintaining competitive task success rates compared with state-of-the-art methods.
authors: Guile Wu, Shuangzhi Li, Xingxin Chen, Chengjie Huang, Sam Hosseini, Tongtong Cao, Yingxue Zhang, Dongfeng Bai
bullets: Addresses high inference latency that limits real-world deployment of world action models.
Adaptively aggregates representations from different world-model layers based on the evolving action-denoising state.
Uses structured action supervision to modulate layer-wise gradients and improve representation learning.
Reduces inference cost by executing fewer world-model layers and caching relevant representations across denoising steps.
Experiments on multiple robot manipulation benchmarks show low latency with competitive task success rates.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes TurboWAM, a fast world action model that reduces inference latency for robot policy learning by aggregating relevant world model representations.
papers.title: TurboWAM: Learning What Matters for Fast World Action Models
papers.tldr: TurboWAM accelerates robot world action models by using only action-relevant world representations while preserving competitive task success.

papers.abstract: Predicting the short-term future trajectory of a person from RGB-D cameras is a key capability for mobile robots navigating in dynamic and human populated environment. The key challenge to deploying learned predictors on real robots is the train-deploy pipeline gap. Training data are often prepared with an idealized, smoothed ground truth, whereas at inference, the model is fed noisy estimates from pose detectors and depth sensors. The model is therefore evaluated on an input distribution it never encountered during training. Most existing models rely on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or transformers, which either struggle to capture short-term temporal dependencies or suffer from computational cost. We present TrajMamba, a lightweight, bidirectional state space model for short-term human trajectory prediction using an RGB-D camera. The model uses a single shared processing path for both training and deployment, aligning human pose extraction, depth back projection, and smoothing processes. It encodes a short window of persons's hip center velocities with stacked bidirectional Mamba blocks and decodes future velocities with a GRU head. On the ETH/UCY benchmark, TrajMamba reaches an average ADE of 0.29 m FDE of 0.51 m. With 262K parameters, it runs in real time on modest hardware and is deployed on a TIAGo robot with an onboard NVIDIA Jetson Orin.
authors: Basheer Al-Tawil, Magnus Jung, Ayoub Al-Hamadi
bullets: Addresses the train-deploy gap caused by idealized training trajectories versus noisy RGB-D pose and depth estimates at inference.
Uses a shared pipeline for pose extraction, depth back projection, and smoothing during both training and deployment.
Encodes recent hip-center velocities with stacked bidirectional Mamba blocks and predicts future velocities using a GRU head.
Achieves 0.29 m average ADE and 0.51 m FDE on ETH/UCY.
Has 262K parameters and runs in real time on modest hardware, including deployment on a TIAGo robot with a Jetson Orin.
papers.selection_reason: Real-time human trajectory prediction for mobile robot navigation in dynamic environments.
papers.title: Real-Time Human Trajectory Prediction from RGB-D for Mobile Robots Using Bi-Mamba
papers.tldr: TrajMamba enables real-time short-term human trajectory prediction for mobile robots by aligning training and deployment inputs with a lightweight bidirectional state space model.

papers.abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection identifies inputs outside the training distribution. Rank-based analyses such as RankFeat and RankWeight suggest that OOD overconfidence is closely related to dominant low-rank components in feature and weight spaces. Since weight averaging operates directly in parameter space and improves model generalization, we consider it for OOD detection from a dominant-component perspective. Trainable Weight Averaging (TWA) assigns a single coefficient to each checkpoint, limiting independent control of dominant weight components. We extend TWA with leading rank-one weight components extracted by Singular Value Decomposition as correction directions, whose contributions are learned through the in-distribution classification objective. On ResNet50, our method improves over fine-tuning and standard TWA across the evaluated datasets with MSP and RankWeight, both with and without Outlier Exposure. Mahalanobis-based evaluation yields mixed results, indicating that the benefit depends on the OOD scoring protocol. Target-layer analyses with MSP and Energy favor correction near the classifier.
authors: Akito Shinohara, Hiroaki Aizawa
bullets: OOD overconfidence is linked to dominant low-rank components in feature and weight spaces.
The method extends Trainable Weight Averaging with SVD-derived rank-one weight corrections learned using the in-distribution classification objective.
On ResNet50, it improves over fine-tuning and standard TWA across evaluated datasets with MSP and RankWeight, with and without Outlier Exposure.
Mahalanobis evaluation is mixed, and target-layer analyses favor applying corrections near the classifier.
papers.selection_reason: Extends Trainable Weight Averaging with rank-one weight components for Out-of-Distribution detection, a method applicable to test-time adaptation and model robustness.
papers.title: Rank-1 Weight-Corrected Trainable Weight Averaging for Out-of-Distribution Detection
papers.tldr: Rank-1 Weight-Corrected TWA improves OOD detection by learning corrections to dominant weight components, though gains depend on the scoring protocol and layer.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can exploit shortcuts, i.e., correlations present in training data that may not hold at test time. This can lead to poor predictions when correlations shift. Most existing solutions for removing shortcuts operate at training time, requiring labeled training data, model weight access, and significant computational resources. Here, we study the problem of test-time shortcut removal. We propose a family of counterfactual test-time augmentation (CTTA) methods: given an example, each method uses an auxiliary model to generate counterfactual edits in which the shortcut value is changed, and then takes a weighted average of the LLM's predictions across these edits. We prove that the optimal shortcut-invariant predictor is a member of this CTTA family, and we characterize its weights. The weights depend on the training distribution, and therefore are, in general, not identifiable from the trained model and unlabeled test data. However, we present assumptions under which the weights can be obtained using the token probabilities of the trained LLM, and propose tests to detect violations of these assumptions. We use these tests to develop Select-CTTA, an aggregate method that selects among CTTA methods. Empirically, we find that Select-CTTA outperforms test-time baselines and approaches the performance of models fine-tuned on shortcut-balanced data.
authors: Katie Matton, Rosalind W. Picard, John Guttag, Maggie Makar
bullets: Addresses shortcut-induced failures under distribution shifts using only test-time intervention, avoiding labeled training data and model-weight access.
Uses an auxiliary model to create counterfactual edits and combines the LLM’s predictions with method-specific weights.
Proves the optimal shortcut-invariant predictor belongs to the CTTA family and characterizes its weights.
Introduces Select-CTTA, which chooses among CTTA methods using tests for assumptions needed to estimate weights from token probabilities.
Empirically, Select-CTTA outperforms test-time baselines and approaches shortcut-balanced fine-tuning performance.
papers.selection_reason: Develops test-time counterfactual augmentation to remove shortcuts in LLM predictions, fitting deployment-time adaptation.
papers.title: Counterfactual Test-Time Augmentation for Shortcut Removal in Language Models
papers.tldr: Counterfactual test-time augmentation reduces language-model shortcut reliance without retraining by averaging predictions over edited examples that change shortcut values.

papers.abstract: Interactive world models hold immense potential for high-stakes applications in robotics, game engines, and immersive digital twins, yet existing benchmarks primarily focus on perceptual similarity rather than the physical-causal coherence essential for real-world utility. We introduce WMEval, a comprehensive benchmark that evaluates interactive world models against Unity-based physical simulations. By leveraging Unity as a high-fidelity ground-truth oracle, we shift evaluation beyond perceptual visual assessment toward the objective state-based verification required for downstream applications. Spanning 9 diverse scenes, WMEval assesses action controllability, scene and character consistency, prompt adherence, kinematics, fluid mechanics, physical causality, and lighting. By executing matched action sequences in both the simulator and the world model, WMEval enables evaluation at both the perceptual level and the physical-causal level, using simulator-derived states as reference. Experiments on state-of-the-art models reveal significant room for improvement in dimensions that remain hidden by standard perceptual metrics but are vital for real-world deployments. Our code is available at: https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/WMEval.
authors: Lanxiang Hu, Yixin Huang, Abhilash Shankarampeta, Zilin Dai, Yuyuan Wu, Kun Qian, Junze Liu, Arvind Srinivasan, Mingjia Huo, Will Lin, Kai Zhong, Weiqi Zhang, Tian Wang, Qingjun Cui, Tajana Rosing, Hao Zhang
bullets: Evaluates world models across 9 diverse scenes using Unity as a high-fidelity ground-truth oracle.
Tests controllability, scene and character consistency, prompt adherence, kinematics, fluid mechanics, physical causality, and lighting.
Runs matched action sequences in both the simulator and world model, comparing perceptual and simulator-derived states.
Finds substantial weaknesses in state-of-the-art models that standard perceptual metrics fail to reveal.
Code is publicly available on GitHub.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces WMEval, a benchmark for evaluating interactive world models against physical simulations, focusing on physical-causal coherence essential for real-world utility.
papers.title: WMEval: Evaluating Interactive World Models Grounded on Physical Simulations
papers.tldr: WMEval benchmarks interactive world models against Unity physics simulations to measure physical-causal correctness beyond visual similarity.

papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting in continual learning (CL) manifests not only as accuracy degradation but also as \emph{explanation drift}: models maintain predictive accuracy while silently shifting attention from diagnostic features to spurious correlations. This work identifies and resolves a previously overlooked structural flaw in explanation-aware CL: pixel-level saliency regularization derives supervision targets from the model's own frozen saliency maps, creating a \emph{self-referential drift loop} that actively reinforces spurious attention across tasks. We introduce \textbf{C$^3$L} (Concept-Consistent Continual Learning), which breaks this loop by anchoring regularization to class-consistent semantic concepts (e.g., ``curved beak'', ``striped pattern'') discovered offline, independent of model state, providing (i) target independence from model drift, and (ii) cross-instance semantic consistency across every instance of a class. We identify that our concept-based objective, combined with approximate LRP relevance conservation, induces a \emph{crowding-out effect}: since concept and background regions compete for the relevance of the same prediction, enforcing high relevance within concept regions implicitly suppresses spurious background correlations without explicit penalization. \method does not require human-annotated concept sets, as it employs a fully automated concept discovery and spatial grounding. Extensive evaluation across five benchmarks and over 20 baselines demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in accuracy, forgetting, explanation quality, spurious correlation mitigation, and out-of-distribution robustness.
authors: Yehonatan Elisha, Oren Barkan, Noam Koenigstein
bullets: Identifies a self-referential drift loop in pixel-level explanation regularization: frozen model saliency maps can reinforce spurious attention across tasks.
Anchors regularization to class-consistent semantic concepts discovered independently of the model, ensuring target independence and cross-instance consistency.
Combines concept-based regularization with approximate LRP relevance conservation, causing relevant concept regions to crowd out spurious background correlations.
Automatically discovers and spatially grounds concepts without human-annotated concept sets.
Across five benchmarks and more than 20 baselines, reports state-of-the-art accuracy, forgetting, explanation quality, spurious-correlation mitigation, and out-of-distribution robustness.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces C$^3$L, a continual learning method that uses semantic concept steering to break the explanation drift loop, offering a novel approach to preventing catastrophic forgetting.
papers.title: Semantic Concept Steering Breaks the Explanation Drift Loop in Continual Learning
papers.tldr: C$^3$L reduces continual-learning forgetting and explanation drift by steering relevance toward stable, automatically discovered semantic concepts rather than self-referential saliency targets.

papers.abstract: Language-aware 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has advanced language-driven 3D scene understanding by incorporating semantic and relational cues into reconstructed scenes. However, relation-aware grounding depends not only on representing such information, but also on whether the underlying scene-side evidence is reliable and sufficient. Multi-view semantic aggregation can incorporate weak observations, while object relations can remain under-observed along the available camera trajectory, leading to ambiguous evidence for target disambiguation. We present RelateGS, a structured language-aware Gaussian representation that selectively refines semantic and relational evidence for 3D visual grounding. RelateGS suppresses unreliable observations during semantic feature uplifting and consolidates multi-view object observations into a persistent 3D graph. The graph further identifies under-observed object relations and guides targeted re-querying of informative existing frames to complement their evidence. Experiments on Sr3D+ and Nr3D demonstrate competitive 3D grounding performance, improving the previous best by 7.9 and 1.7 percentage points at Acc@0.25, respectively.
authors: Seongjun Choi, Sangyoun Lee
bullets: Addresses ambiguous target disambiguation caused by weak semantic observations and incomplete relational evidence.
Suppresses unreliable multi-view observations during semantic feature uplifting.
Builds a persistent 3D object-relation graph from multi-view observations.
Uses the graph to identify missing relations and re-query informative existing frames.
Improves prior best Acc@0.25 by 7.9 points on Sr3D+ and 1.7 points on Nr3D.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes RelateGS, a language-aware Gaussian Splatting method for 3D scene understanding and visual grounding, contributing to 3D foundation models and spatial reasoning.
papers.title: RelateGS: Reliable Semantic and Relational Evidence for 3D Scene Understanding with Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: RelateGS improves language-driven 3D grounding by filtering unreliable semantic evidence and actively strengthening under-observed object relations in Gaussian-splat scenes.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to follow instructions in typed text, limiting broader deployment in natural speech. The traditional solution by prepending a speech recognition before VLA to convert speech into texts would incur additional latency and propagate errors. To address this, we present Speech-$\pi_{0.5}$, which maps raw speech directly to motor commands without explicit textual transcriptions. Specifically, built on $\pi_{0.5}$, we use a cross-modal projection to convert voice frames directly into audio tokens with significant response latency reduction. To further improve the accuracy, we adopt split LoRA adaptation with dedicated audio and task adapters, under a two-stage training. Speech-$\pi_{0.5}$ achieves $3\times$ lower response latency than ASR pipeline while maintaining competitive task success on LIBERO, and generalizes robustly to unseen accents where a single adapter degrades significantly.
authors: Enfu Nan, Pu Zhao, Yixiao Chen, Lin Zhao, Juyi Lin, Chen Wang, Weiwei Chen, Yanzhi Wang
bullets: VLA robots typically require typed instructions or an intermediate speech-recognition step.
The proposed model directly converts speech into motor commands, avoiding transcription latency and error propagation.
A cross-modal projection produces audio tokens, while split LoRA adapters separately handle audio and task adaptation.
The system achieves 3× lower response latency than an ASR-based pipeline with competitive LIBERO task success.
It generalizes robustly to unseen accents, unlike a single-adapter approach.
papers.selection_reason: Presents Speech-$ ackslash$pi$_{0.5}$, a model for robotic manipulation that maps raw speech directly to motor commands, advancing vision-language-action models for embodied agents.
papers.title: Late Breaking Results: Audio-Language-Action Models with Direct Speech Conditioning for Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: Speech-π₀.₅ maps raw speech directly to robotic actions, reducing response latency while maintaining task performance and robustness to accents.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires actions whose validity depends on earlier interactions, yet visual progress can conceal missing task prerequisites. We propose RoboLongR, an offline-to-online framework that learns history-dependent rewards to guide policy adaptation to new tasks. Its central objective is causal consistency: aligning rewarded progress with prerequisites supported by execution history. Stage-shuffle supervision encourages execution-order sensitivity, recurrent memory preserves evidence of earlier interactions, and two-round training refines trajectory segments using predicted progress. The resulting rewards guide stage-conditioned policy refinement from behavior cloning to online reinforcement learning. Sparse terminal feedback connects policy experience to reward learning by triggering correction for repeated high-scoring failures. Pretrained on demonstrations from 88 RLBench tasks and Open-X data, RoboLongR achieves 31.8% average success on 18 long-horizon tasks excluded from reward pretraining, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 9.2 percentage points. Across four real-robot tasks, it achieves 57.5% success, a 32.5-percentage-point improvement over the comparison method. Reward-level controls probe sensitivity to synthetic order perturbations, while ablations examine the contributions of individual components to policy improvement.
authors: Zixuan Chen, Lin Cao, Fenggang Zhang, Haotong Zhang, Yangtao Chen, Jieqi Shi, Jing Huo, Yang Gao
bullets: Addresses failures where visual progress hides missing prerequisites from earlier interactions.
Uses stage-shuffle supervision, recurrent memory, and two-round trajectory refinement to model execution order and history.
Guides adaptation from behavior cloning to online reinforcement learning, with sparse terminal feedback correcting repeated failures.
Achieves 31.8% average success on 18 held-out long-horizon tasks, 9.2 percentage points above the strongest evaluated baseline.
Reaches 57.5% success across four real-robot tasks, improving by 32.5 percentage points over the comparison method.
papers.selection_reason: History-dependent reward learning for long-horizon robot manipulation.
papers.title: RoboLongR: Causally Consistent Rewards Teach Robots to Progressively Master Long-Horizon Manipulation
papers.tldr: RoboLongR learns causally consistent, history-dependent rewards to help robots master long-horizon manipulation through progressive policy refinement.

papers.abstract: We introduce TrackTok, an efficient video tokenization framework that produces object-centric tokens, i.e., tokens that consistently encode the same semantic objects across time, even as it moves, deforms, or undergoes partial occlusion. Conventional patch-based or existing holistic tokenizers produce token identities often tied to fixed image locations. In contrast, our approach learns temporally persistent object-centric representations that bind visual features across frames into stable semantic units. This enables substantially more compact, continuous latent video representations, reducing the number of tokens required for downstream generative modeling with state-of-the-art flow models, while preserving the semantic structure needed for high-quality synthesis. Our tokenizer offers a favorable quality-efficiency trade-off. TrackTok achieves comparable class-conditional generative FVD on UCF-101 dataset at 8 times fewer latent tokens and better latency, and outperforms existing 1D tokenization baselines on frame prediction task on Kinetics-600 across low token budgets. These results suggest that object-aligned and temporally persistent tokenization is a promising direction for scalable video generation, where reducing latent token counts is critical for efficient modeling. Our code for this work is available at https://github.com/phamleyennhi/tracktok.
authors: Nhi Pham, Christopher Wewer, Bernt Schiele, Jonas Fischer, Jan Eric Lenssen
bullets: Addresses the instability of patch-based and holistic tokens whose identities are tied to fixed image locations.
Learns tokens that track the same objects across motion, deformation, and partial occlusion.
Produces compact continuous latent representations for downstream flow-based video generation.
Matches class-conditional FVD on UCF-101 with 8× fewer latent tokens and lower latency.
Outperforms 1D tokenization baselines on Kinetics-600 frame prediction at low token budgets.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces object-centric video tokenization that reduces token count for efficient video generation and understanding, directly addressing token efficiency and video representation.
papers.title: TrackTok: Object-Centric Video Tokenization with Semantically Persistent Tokens
papers.tldr: TrackTok tokenizes videos into semantically persistent object-centric tokens, enabling efficient generation with far fewer latent tokens while maintaining video quality.

papers.abstract: Language is a natural way to command robots, but converting a single instruction into a long-horizon, contact-rich hand-object interaction remains challenging: synthesized references are noisy, human-to-robot retargeting introduces embodiment bias, and fixed-reference tracking lets small errors snowball. We address this with AdaDexTrack, a modulator-in-the-loop framework for language-conditioned manipulation tracking. A distilled generalist tracker serves as the skill carrier, while a tightly aligned modulator performs three feedback corrections: reference modulation (continual adjustment of what to track), object-latent modulation (online adaptation of the object representation to recruit suitable skills), and positional-target modulation (small state-dependent refinements for execution). The tracker is learned via large-scale specialist to generalist distillation on a corpus of language-conditioned hand-object trajectories; the modulator is trained with RL under the same task objective, ensuring tight coupling. Across large-scale evaluations, AdaDexTrack consistently outperforms prior SOTA on unseen-trajectory and unseen-object sets in both average tracking error and success rate, demonstrating robustness and generalization. We further show zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on real hardware, where adding the modulator yields substantial gains over a tracker-only variant. AdaDexTrack reframes language-conditioned dexterous manipulation as modulated tracking, replacing the open-loop, fixed-reference tracking with in-loop modulation that adjusts the reference, object latent, and positional target, yielding drift-resistant execution from noisy text references.
authors: Jianibieke Adalibieke, Qianwei Han, Xueyi Liu, Yuzhe Qin, Li Yi
bullets: Addresses noisy language-generated references, embodiment bias, and error accumulation in long-horizon contact-rich manipulation.
Combines a distilled generalist tracker with an RL-trained, tightly coupled modulator.
The modulator performs reference, object-latent, and positional-target feedback corrections.
Outperforms prior state of the art on unseen trajectories and objects in tracking error and success rate.
Demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, with modulation substantially improving over tracker-only execution.
papers.selection_reason: Language-conditioned dexterous manipulation tracking with in-loop modulation.
papers.title: AdaDexTrack: Dynamic Modulation for Adaptive and Generalizable Dexterous Manipulation Tracking
papers.tldr: AdaDexTrack improves language-conditioned dexterous manipulation by dynamically modulating tracking references, object representations, and target positions during execution.

papers.abstract: Video world models (VWMs) are rapidly emerging as scalable neural simulators for robotic manipulation. However, most benchmarks only evaluate them as open-world video generators, using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that lack strict 3D spatial and kinematic reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce RoboWorM, a comprehensive, deployment-aware benchmark that leverages known hardware priors such as robot kinematic trees and fixed camera configurations, to systematically examine structural and spatiotemporal fidelity. RoboWorM curates 1,605 episodes across single-arm, bimanual, and humanoid morphologies, spanning both Markovian and long-horizon non-Markovian tasks under single- and multi-view setups. To explicitly measure physical consistency, we propose two deterministic, VLM-free metrics: KIVA for intra-view kinematic stability, and RIGIS for multi-view geometric consistency. By exploiting intrinsic robotic invariants, KIVA improves hallucination detection alignment with human annotations by 25.8% relative to the strongest frontier VLMs, while RIGIS achieves a 130% higher Spearman correlation with human preferences. Furthermore, since real-world deployment requires low inference latency, we utilize RoboWorM to conduct the first large-scale audit of the quality-efficiency trade-off. Evaluating 9 state-of-the-art acceleration techniques across 3 leading world models (over 29,000 generated rollouts), we demonstrate how these acceleration methods can retain superficial visual quality while silently compromising deployment-critical physical constraints. Using our metrics, we achieve 2.3$\times$ maximum inference speed-up with minimal quality loss.
authors: Doanh Le Thien, Viet-Thanh Nguyen, Pham Tri Quang, Nhi Pham, Christopher Wewer, Minh-Loi Nguyen, Hoang H. Tran, Tho Le, Tung M. Luu, Dung D. Le, Vu N. Duong, Jonas Fischer, Ngan Le, An Thai Le, Daniel Sonntag, Gim Hee Lee, James Zou, Mathias Niepert, Jan Peters, Duy M. H. Nguyen, Ngo Anh Vien
bullets: Introduces a deployment-aware benchmark covering 1,605 episodes across single-arm, bimanual, and humanoid robots, with single- and multi-view, short- and long-horizon tasks.
Proposes VLM-free metrics: KIVA for intra-view kinematic stability and RIGIS for multi-view geometric consistency.
KIVA and RIGIS align more closely with human judgments than frontier VLMs, improving correlation by 25.8% and 130%, respectively.
Audits 9 acceleration methods across 3 world models and over 29,000 rollouts, showing that visual quality can remain high while physical consistency degrades.
Finds up to 2.3× inference speed-up with minimal measured quality loss.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark and metrics for physical consistency in embodied video world models.
papers.title: RoboWorM: Evaluating Movement Realism, Consistency and Acceleration Affects in Embodied Video World Models
papers.tldr: RoboWorM benchmarks whether robotic video world models generate physically consistent, deployment-ready motion—not merely visually plausible videos.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have become strong visual reasoners, yet remain limited in open-world, multi-step search that requires grounding images, selecting tools, and integrating web evidence. Existing approaches typically construct and filter fixed offline corpora whose question distributions cannot adapt as the target deep-search agent improves. Building on MTA-Agent's image-grounded QA construction, we present MTA-Zero, an online multimodal QA-Solver co-training framework for self-improving multimodal deep-search agents that requires no precomputed multi-hop corpus. Starting from image-grounded VQA seed contexts, a trainable QA Generator retrieves evidence and constructs verified multi-hop questions online. A separate deep-search Solver then selects tools, gathers evidence, and answers the generated questions. To focus generation on the Solver's learning frontier, we derive a Goldilocks reward for the QA Generator from the Solver's group-wise rollout success rate: questions solved by all rollouts or by none receive zero reward, whereas questions near the current frontier are favored. We optimize the two policies independently with GRPO, without sharing parameters or gradients. Across six multimodal deep-search benchmarks, MTA-Zero improves a Qwen3-VL-8B Solver from 36.91% to 51.58% mean accuracy and achieves performance comparable to GPT-5 under the same agent workflow. The same framework also improves a newer Qwen3.6-27B Solver by 10.82 points. These results show that verified online question generation provides a policy-specific curriculum for continually improving multimodal deep-search agents.
authors: Xiangyu Peng, Jiaxin Zhang, An Yan, Yu Li, Ran Xu, Zeyuan Chen, Chien-Sheng Wu
bullets: Addresses the rigidity of fixed offline training corpora for open-world, multi-step multimodal search.
Generates verified, image-grounded multi-hop questions online using retrieved evidence.
Uses a Goldilocks reward to prioritize questions at the Solver’s current learning frontier.
Independently trains the QA Generator and deep-search Solver with GRPO, without shared parameters or gradients.
Improves Qwen3-VL-8B from 36.91% to 51.58% mean accuracy across six benchmarks; also boosts Qwen3.6-27B by 10.82 points.
papers.selection_reason: Online co-training framework for self-improving multimodal deep-search agents built on MLLMs; relevant to multimodal LLM agent training.
papers.title: MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA-Solver Co-training
papers.tldr: MTA-Zero continually improves multimodal deep-search agents by generating and verifying challenging multi-hop questions online while co-training a question generator and search solver.

papers.abstract: Deploying a language-guided navigation policy in a new building usually means watching it fail. Public-benchmark VLAs degrade scene by scene as layout, appearance, and language drift, and the standard fix of teleoperating fresh trajectories on site does not scale. We replace human demonstration with a single brief iPhone scan. Scan2Instruction compiles that scan into a complete training environment, automatically synthesizing executable navigation episodes with grounded instructions. PRPT-KS then adapts the policy through a closed-form Pareto utility read directly off the reconstructed scene, with no learned critic and no human labels. Across five real environments, the two designs together drive our RealNav to an 85% real-robot success rate, compared with 49% for a RealNav baseline post-trained on human demonstrations, and still achieve 82% in unscanned regions of the same buildings, compared with 41% for the same baseline. Our work turns demonstration-free scene adaptation for language-guided navigation from an aspiration into a working reality.
authors: Zhuoyuan Yu, Yuxing Long, Du Wang, Junyang Wang, Hongwei Fan, Hao Dong
bullets: Addresses policy degradation under changes in building layout, appearance, and language.
Scan2Instruction converts one scan into a complete training environment with executable, grounded navigation episodes.
PRPT-KS adapts the policy using a closed-form Pareto utility derived from the reconstructed scene, without a learned critic.
Across five real environments, the approach reaches 85% success in scanned areas and 82% in unscanned regions.
The abstract reports higher success than human-demonstration post-training baselines: 49% and 41%, respectively.
papers.selection_reason: Demonstration-free adaptation of language-guided navigation using a single scene scan; directly in vision-language navigation.
papers.title: One Scan is Enough: Demonstration-Free Adaptation for Language-Guided Navigation
papers.tldr: A single brief iPhone scan can adapt a language-guided navigation policy to a new building without human demonstrations or labels, achieving 85% real-robot success across five environments.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance when integrated into robot manipulation pipelines, but real-world evaluation of VLM capabilities on downstream robotics tasks is both difficult and expensive to scale. We propose that spatial and temporal ordering tasks using images from stereo and wrist cameras attached to real-world robots are particularly well-suited for evaluating visual reasoning capabilities, as they assess skills directly applicable to robots. We evaluate VLM reasoning abilities on three questions: ordering shuffled frames conditioned on a language description of the task, ordering objects depthwise based on distance from the camera, and ordering objects from left-to-right in pixel coordinates. The complexity of these tasks can also be modulated by changing the size of the set to sort. Our experiments show that several state-of-the-art vision-language models struggle on ordering tasks. To fix this, we propose a scalable autonomous training data generation pipeline, and show that both supervised finetuning and reinforcement-learning on the generated data can significantly improve VLM reasoning performance both on spatiotemporal ordering tasks as well as downstream robotics and visual reasoning tasks.
authors: Sagnik Anupam, Utkarsh Lal, Aneesh Edara, Botong Zhang, Yao Tang, Jiatao Gu, Dinesh Jayaraman, Osbert Bastani
bullets: Evaluates VLMs on language-conditioned frame ordering, depthwise object ordering, and left-to-right pixel-coordinate ordering.
Uses stereo and wrist-camera images from real-world robots, with task difficulty controlled by the number of items to sort.
Finds that several state-of-the-art VLMs struggle with these robotics-relevant ordering problems.
Introduces an autonomous pipeline for generating scalable training data.
Shows that supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on this data improve ordering performance and transfer to downstream robotics and visual reasoning tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Improves VLM spatiotemporal and depth-ordering reasoning for robotics via generated data; fits spatial intelligence and embodied reasoning.
papers.title: RoboReason: Boosting Robotics-Relevant VLM Reasoning Through Scalable Data Generation
papers.tldr: RoboReason introduces scalable robot-camera ordering tasks and synthetic training data to improve VLM spatial and temporal reasoning for robotics.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets large language models (LLMs) answer knowledge-intensive questions from retrieved evidence, but adapting a general-purpose RAG system to a specialized domain such as medicine is difficult when only an unlabeled corpus is available. Self-training approaches such as SimRAG address this by letting the LLM write its own question-answer pairs from domain passages and fine-tuning on the pairs that survive a round-trip consistency filter. We observe that these approaches treat every retained example identically: they never ask whether the student already knows the answer, already extracts it correctly from the retrieved context, or fails - and if so, whether the failure lies with the reader or with the retriever. To tackle this, we propose TriageRAG, a failure-aware self-training approach that probes the student on each self-generated question with and without retrieved context, triages it into one of four categories (known, solved, context-failure, retrieval-failure), and routes each category to the training signal that addresses it, including a parametric route that teaches the reader to answer when retrieval misses. Probing is cheap and repeated every round, so the training mixture follows the student, and the triage histogram doubles as a label-free diagnostic of where the domain gap lies. Experiments on 11 datasets spanning three domains with a Qwen3-4B backbone, and on CS-Bench with Qwen3-8B, demonstrate that TriageRAG outperforms a budget-matched SimRAG by 1.2-6.4 points and is the only method that recovers the closed-book level in every case where retrieval hurts the base model. A single ablation identifies the mechanism: round-trip filtering removes every training context that lacks the evidence, and a reader that never sees such contexts learns to over-trust noisy retrieval.
authors: Samarth Varshney, Ritu Yadav
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of adapting RAG to specialized domains using only unlabeled corpora.
Probes answers with and without retrieved context, categorizing examples as known, solved, context-failure, or retrieval-failure.
Routes each category to reader, retriever, or parametric training signals; repeated probing adapts the mixture to the student.
Evaluated across 11 datasets in three domains and CS-Bench, it improves over budget-matched SimRAG by 1.2–6.4 points.
The method recovers closed-book performance whenever retrieval harms the base model; filtering out evidence-lacking contexts can cause readers to over-trust retrieval.
papers.selection_reason: Failure-aware self-training for adapting retrieval-augmented LLMs to specialized domains; relevant to language foundation model adaptation.
papers.title: TriageRAG: Failure-Aware Self-Training for Adapting Retrieval-Augmented Language Models to Specialized Domains
papers.tldr: TriageRAG improves unlabeled-domain adaptation of RAG systems by diagnosing why each self-generated example fails and applying a targeted training signal.

papers.abstract: Users of conversational assistants rarely state all requirements up front: they add constraints, amend them, withdraw them, digress, and return. Instruction-tuned LLMs fail here in two ways: active constraints stop being honored as turns accumulate (persistence failure), and withdrawn constraints keep being enacted (relapse). The only existing repair we know of is an external ledger that re-injects a compiled specification every turn. We propose StateWise, a self-improving approach that teaches a single LLM to maintain its own revisable constraint state, a typed state with tombstones for revoked constraints, so persistence and relapse are measured by executable checkers and ground-truth states are compiled for free. StateWise fine-tunes the LLM on two complementary skills, summarizing a dialogue into its constraint state and responding conditioned on that state, then self-trains on its own trajectories, keeping only turns that pass an exact round-trip check against the compiled state. This teaches 7-8B models to track the state almost perfectly but, surprisingly, not to obey it: on Llama-3.1-8B every supervised variant roughly doubles relapse. We therefore add a preference stage on self-generated relapse contrasts, where the rejected response enacts a revoked rule and the chosen one passes the round-trip check. On two backbones with held-out constraint families and unseen phrasings, StateWise cuts relapse by 8-22 points relative to supervised self-training, lifts conversation success by 8-19 points over the backbone, and beats an oracle compiled-ledger baseline on relapse with no inference-time scaffolding. We also characterize the recipe's cost on general instruction-following benchmarks and study weight interpolation as a mitigation.
authors: Samarth Varshney, Ritu Yadav
bullets: Addresses persistence failures, where active constraints are forgotten, and relapse, where withdrawn constraints are still followed.
Uses a typed, revisable constraint state with tombstones, plus exact round-trip checks against automatically compiled ground-truth states.
Combines supervised state summarization and state-conditioned response training with preference learning from self-generated relapse contrasts.
Across two backbones, it reduces relapse by 8–22 points versus supervised self-training and improves conversation success by 8–19 points over the base models.
The approach has costs on general instruction-following benchmarks; weight interpolation is explored as a mitigation.
papers.selection_reason: Teaches LLMs to track and obey evolving constraints in multi-turn dialogue, contributing to LLM reasoning and state tracking.
papers.title: StateWise: Teaching Language Models to Track and Obey Evolving Constraints in Multi-Turn Dialogue
papers.tldr: StateWise trains language models to maintain and obey changing dialogue constraints, reducing both forgotten active rules and reactivated revoked rules without an external ledger.

papers.abstract: Embodied perception requires positional representations that capture both physical geometry and the spatial and temporal extent of observations. We introduce POD-RoPE (Physical Observation Distribution RoPE), which represents token observation footprints as distributions over camera centers, viewing directions, and sampling times. Under independent sampling, expected rotations encode relative relationships between distributions; when each distribution collapses to a single address, the construction recovers pointwise RoPE. The same rotation statistics support Q/K matching and coherence-dependent V/O transformations, allowing observation geometry to guide both information selection and content aggregation. Per-token pre-aggregation avoids increasing sequence length or processing pairs of observation nodes. We evaluate POD-RoPE across four robot policy architectures, simulation and real-world manipulation, and complementary reconstruction, depth-estimation, and novel-view-synthesis tasks. Integrating POD-RoPE into Fast-WAM improves mean success from 91.83% to 92.88% across all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, and from 32.5% to 52.5% on two real-robot tasks on Sharpa North. Controlled reconstruction ablations support the contributions of distribution encoding and V/O transformations. In H20 model-block benchmarks, POD-RoPE achieves median forward-plus-backward speedups of $1.91\times$ over P-RoPE and $5.34\times$ over RayRoPE, with a median latency overhead of 17.4% over Standard RoPE. These results support physical observation distributions as an effective and computationally efficient basis for geometry-aware attention.
authors: Xiaodi Huang, Zilin Wang, Jinpeng Liu, Pengchuan Xiao, Zhenlei Shao, Zhang Zhang, Shuxiang Lu
bullets: Represents each token’s observation footprint as distributions over camera centers, viewing directions, and sampling times.
Uses distribution-derived rotation statistics for geometric Q/K matching and coherence-dependent V/O content aggregation; pointwise RoPE is recovered for single-address observations.
Pre-aggregation incorporates observation geometry without processing pairs of observation nodes or increasing sequence length.
Evaluated across four robot-policy architectures, simulation and real-world manipulation, plus reconstruction, depth estimation, and novel-view synthesis.

Fast-WAM performance improved from 91.83% to 92.88% across 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks and from 32.5% to 52.5% on two real-robot tasks; it also outpaced P-RoPE and RayRoPE in H20 benchmarks, with 17.4% median latency overhead over Standard RoPE.
papers.selection_reason: Geometry-aware rotary position encoding for embodied perception and robot policies.
papers.title: POD-RoPE: Rotary Position Encoding over Physical Observation Distributions for Embodied AI
papers.tldr: POD-RoPE encodes the physical extent of embodied observations into attention rotations, improving geometry-aware perception and robot manipulation while avoiding sequence-length growth.

papers.abstract: Floor traction influences wheel-slip behavior, dead-reckoning accuracy, and the navigation performance of wheeled mobile robots that rely on wheel odometry. As these robots become increasingly common in GNSS-denied indoor environments, including automated manufacturing and retail facilities, their onboard measurements could also be used to characterize floor conditions and improve localization. In this study, a skid-steer robot was driven over five floor surfaces with distinct traction characteristics using commanded velocity profiles designed to induce wheel slip through repeated acceleration and direction reversal. Differences between the body velocity estimated from inertial sensing and the velocity obtained from wheel odometry were evaluated using the integrated relative-velocity error, phase-derived wheel-to-body response delay, and velocity-reversal response delay. Welch power spectral density analysis was additionally applied to characterize the frequency distribution of the velocity mismatch during positive and negative acceleration. Band-integrated spectral power, spectral centroid, and spectral decay rate were extracted from each recording and evaluated using linear discriminant analysis and multiclass classification. The response-delay measurements produced consistent surface-dependent trends, with the longest delays observed on soap and the shortest delays observed on carpet. The spectral features also provided clear separation among the tested surfaces, achieving a balanced classification accuracy of 97.1% under recording-level cross-validation. These results demonstrate that both the magnitude and frequency domain characteristics of wheel-to-body velocity mismatch contain useful information about tire-surface interactions. Such information could support surface recognition and the development of slip-aware wheel-odometry weighting within robot state-estimation frameworks.
authors: Kulbhushan Komarraju, Nathaniel Pearson, Yu Gu, Jason Gross
bullets: Floor traction affects wheel slip, wheel-odometry accuracy, and indoor robot navigation.
The robot was driven with acceleration and reversal maneuvers designed to induce slip on five distinct surfaces.
Researchers compared inertial body velocity with wheel odometry using integrated error, response delays, and Welch power-spectral features.
Response delays varied by surface, with the longest on soap and shortest on carpet.
Time- and frequency-domain mismatch features separated the surfaces and could support slip-aware localization and odometry weighting.
papers.selection_reason: Wheel-slip-based surface classification supports slip-aware odometry and localization for wheeled robot navigation.
papers.title: Floor Friction Assessment from Robot Tire-Surface Interaction
papers.tldr: A skid-steer robot can identify floor traction conditions from wheel–body velocity mismatch, achieving 97.1% balanced classification accuracy across five tested surfaces.

papers.abstract: Many robot manipulation videos do not indicate whether the task was successfully completed. RoboJev-27B is an open-weight vision-language model that takes a task instruction, 10 frames of a manipulation attempt, and (if available) final frames from auxiliary cameras and predicts whether the robot accomplished the task. RoboJev-27B is a variant of JEV-27B-VL, trained with a rank-32 LoRA adapter on the language model only (keeping the vision encoder frozen) using 52,598 episode records. It also uses a source-specific KL penalty that applies only to research data, anchoring predictions closer to the original model on those sources. It uses a calibrated two-token readout that outputs success/failure probabilities in a single forward pass. On 268 held-out episodes of the same robot model (SO-101), RoboJev-27B attains 95.2% balanced accuracy and 0.993 AUROC. It also generalises to episodes collected by unseen labs/robots (AUROC = 0.890 over 459 episodes) as well as to clearly labelled community-collected episodes (accuracy = 93.3% over 135 episodes), where the base model attains an AUROC = 0.900 on the unseen-lab/robot subset with the same inputs. It takes 0.26 seconds per episode (median, serial) to infer on a single H100, which is about \$0.19 per 1,000 success predictions at \$2.69 per GPU-hour (not including media processing and serving costs). RoboJev-27B is released together with its inference code, along with a transparent evaluation: 20,628 predictions organized into 29 model/protocol entries are made available to facilitate browsing and to enable reproducible benchmarking of success detection. We also compare against strong API-based frontier VLMs, which take in fewer input frames (4 images from the primary camera only); note that this comparison is not strictly like-for-like because RoboJev-27B is given more frames at inference.
authors: Josef Liyanjun Chen
bullets: Addresses the lack of success labels in many robot manipulation videos.
Fine-tunes JEV-27B-VL with a language-only LoRA adapter, frozen vision encoder, source-specific KL regularization, and a calibrated two-token success/failure readout.
Uses 10 manipulation frames plus optional auxiliary-camera final frames as input.
Reports 95.2% balanced accuracy and 0.993 AUROC on held-out SO-101 episodes; cross-lab/robot AUROC is 0.890.
Released with inference code and 20,628 predictions across 29 evaluation entries for reproducible benchmarking; comparisons with frontier VLMs use fewer frames and are not strictly like-for-like.
papers.selection_reason: Open vision-language judge for robot success detection from manipulation videos.
papers.title: RoboJev: An Open Vision-Language Judge for Robot Success Detection
papers.tldr: RoboJev-27B is an open vision-language model that judges robot manipulation success from task instructions and video frames, achieving strong in-domain and cross-domain performance.

papers.abstract: A robot in a home it has never seen must open doors, drawers, lids and taps whose physics a picture does not show. Instructions such as "open the drawer halfway, gently" depend on that physics: how far a part travels, how it resists, and what locks it. We present Open-World Law-to-Action (L2A). A vision-language model (VLM) proposes, for each movable part, its motions, the terms of its law of motion, and what may lock it. Each proposal becomes a prior with a floor, so that touch can always overturn it. The robot identifies each part's law online by Bayesian linear regression with closed-form evidence, for parts that move in one way or in two, and keeps a hypothesis that an unseen part or motion locks the target. We prove that touch alone cannot rule this hypothesis out, derive when another look is worth its cost, and show that a constant load and friction cannot be told apart while a part moves one way. All experiments are in simulation, developed on some scenes and run once on held-out ones. In new kitchens the robot completes 80% of tasks from the VLM's proposals, against 98% when every part is known. Proposed physics raises success on objects that need new terms from 353 to 378-383 of 400 episodes, and a second look raises success in mixed scenes from 284 to 329 of 366 tasks. A mobile robot that takes nothing from the simulator completes 70 of 100 requests in new scenes, against 62 when the simulator says which part each box is (after one change made between two held-out tests).
authors: Mohamed A. Mabrok
bullets: Targets open-world tasks such as opening doors, drawers, lids, and taps according to force- and motion-sensitive instructions.
A VLM proposes part motions, motion-law terms, and possible locks; touch can revise these priors online.
Bayesian linear regression identifies one- or two-way motion laws while maintaining an unseen-lock hypothesis.
The analysis characterizes limits of touch-only identification and when an additional visual observation is worthwhile.
In simulation, proposed physics and second looks improve held-out task success; a mobile robot completes 70/100 requests in new scenes.],
papers.selection_reason: Vision-language priors combined with touch for open-world robot manipulation of parts with hidden physics.
papers.title: Open-World Law-to-Action: Vision-Language Priors and Touch for Parts with Hidden Physics
papers.tldr: L2A combines vision-language physics priors with touch-based Bayesian identification to manipulate unfamiliar articulated objects under hidden physical constraints.

papers.abstract: Typed decision-making tasks in agents, such as UI element selection, product recommendation, and chart matching, require models to choose from a set of discrete candidates. While prior work demonstrates that text-only System One models achieve four key properties including candidate-order invariance, scalability, and cache reuse via separate request-candidate encoding, extending them to multimodal settings where candidates are visual remains underexplored. We introduce Iris, a framework that accommodates image, text, or hybrid candidates while preserving the core decision module. We prove that order invariance and exact cache reuse hold for any per-candidate encoder under Iris, and derive the closed-form latency reduction. We construct a visual-candidate benchmark from Multimodal-Mind2Web (K=16, deduplicated, order-shuffled, three generalization splits). Independent encoding (Iris) achieves 78.4 / 72.1 / 74.8 percent accuracy with zero-flip rate under candidate reordering. Joint encoding reaches 90.6 / 89.5 / 91.6 percent but suffers an 8 to 10 percent answer-flip rate when shuffled. To bridge this gap, we propose a design that encodes each candidate conditioned on the request state without inter-candidate cross-attention; it preserves strict order invariance, enables forked cache sharing, and attains 91.7 / 86.5 / 90.0 percent accuracy at one-third of OneJev latency with calibrated null probabilities (AUROC 0.93 to 0.97). Reusing image candidates across requests cuts latency by 37x at K=256 and 191x at K=2048. On MetaEncoder benchmarks, Iris-4B achieves 100 percent on JevBench original and easy, outperforming 30B MetaEncoder and 27B OpenJev. Finally, we resolve a systems bottleneck on Ampere GPUs: reformulating Qwen3.5 patch-embedding Conv3d into its exact matrix-product form accelerates processing by 350x. Code, data, and checkpoints: https://github.com/lllfx/Iris.
authors: Fengxin Li
bullets: Targets typed-choice tasks such as UI selection, recommendation, and chart matching with visual candidates.
Uses per-candidate encoding, including request-conditioned encoding without inter-candidate cross-attention, to preserve strict order invariance and reusable caches.
The proposed design reaches 91.7/86.5/90.0% accuracy across three splits, with one-third of OneJev’s latency and AUROC 0.93–0.97 for calibrated null probabilities.
Reusing image candidates reduces latency by 37× at K=256 and 191× at K=2048.
An exact Conv3d-to-matrix-product reformulation accelerates Qwen3.5 patch embedding by 350× on Ampere GPUs.
papers.selection_reason: Multimodal decision framework with order-invariant candidate encoding and reusable inference cache; relevant to memory-efficient inference and latency reduction.
papers.title: Seeing the Options: Typed Decisions over Visual Candidates with Reusable Option Memory
papers.tldr: Iris enables order-invariant, cacheable decisions over visual, textual, or hybrid candidates while achieving strong accuracy and major latency savings.

papers.abstract: Unrolled variational networks achieve state-of-the-art performance for accelerated MRI reconstruction, but standard end-to-end training becomes prohibitively memory intensive as the number and width of cascades increase. We propose a memory-efficient training framework that updates a randomly sampled cascade while retaining supervision from the final reconstruction loss. The error signal is propagated from the end of the chain to the sampled cascade using an activation-light backward pass that avoids storing full chain activations, thereby decoupling training memory from chain length. A time-conditioned network shared across cascades further keeps the parameter count independent of chain length. The backward pass is approximate only through frozen normalization statistics, and a trained exact gradient control shows the approximation leaves reconstruction quality unchanged. The framework remains trainable at chain lengths and cascade widths where standard end-to-end backpropagation exhausts GPU memory. On fastMRI single-coil knee and multi-coil brain reconstruction, our method consistently outperforms other local training approaches. On high-SNR knee slices, our method surpasses E2E-VarNet at $8\times$ and matches it at $4\times$, while on the complete brain validation set it surpasses E2E-VarNet at $8\times$ and achieves comparable performance at $4\times$, with fewer parameters, lower peak memory, and faster per-iteration training. Code is available at https://github.com/emehillaj/scalable-unrolled-mri.
authors: Emiljo M\"ehillaj, Ender Konukoglu
bullets: Randomly samples a cascade for updating while retaining supervision from the final reconstruction loss.
Uses an activation-light backward pass to propagate error without memory scaling with chain length.
Shares a time-conditioned network across cascades, keeping parameter count independent of chain length.
Maintains reconstruction quality despite approximate gradients caused by frozen normalization statistics.
Outperforms other local-training methods and matches or exceeds E2E-VarNet in the reported fastMRI knee and brain settings, with fewer parameters, lower peak memory, and faster iteration training.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a memory-efficient training framework for unrolled variational networks in MRI reconstruction, fitting 3D Vision and Efficient AI.
papers.title: Scalable Unrolled Chains for MRI Reconstruction
papers.tldr: A memory-efficient training framework makes very deep and wide unrolled MRI reconstruction networks trainable without storing activations from the full cascade chain.

papers.abstract: Whole Slide Image (WSI) analysis serves as the fundamental method for the clinical diagnosis of cancer in digital histopathology. Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have enabled state-of-the-art (SOTA) automated histopathology report generation. However, MLLMs reason purely through distributions encoded in their neural parameters, limiting the amount of knowledge and reasoning logic they can contain given the model scale. Their black-box reasoning poses another challenge to the human interpretation of intermediate reasoning. We address these issues by utilizing knowledge graphs to inject external structured knowledge for MLLMs to reason over, while making this reasoning component visible. Knowledge graphs are capable of partially externalizing the containment of medical knowledge, an area that remains underexplored in pathology report generation. We introduce PathKGen, a knowledge graph-assisted MLLM for histopathology report generation. PathKGen has two main branches: (1) a visual path that learns visual token inputs to the MLLM using pathology foundation models, and (2) a knowledge path that learns knowledge token inputs by extracting key morphological features of WSIs through querying a pathology-specific knowledge graph. A comprehensive evaluation on WSI-Bench dataset shows that PathKGen surpasses previous SOTA methods while revealing diagnostic reasoning as visually intuitive graphs. Due to its modular design, the proposed knowledge path is complementary to vision-aligned MLLMs and can be extended to other applications by curating domain-specific knowledge graphs to generate knowledge tokens.
authors: Nadun Rajapaksha, Sandun Herath, Devnith Wijesinghe, Isiri Amani Withanawasam, Hasindri Watawana, Ranga Rodrigo
bullets: Targets limited embedded knowledge and opaque reasoning in MLLMs for whole-slide image analysis.
Uses a visual branch with pathology foundation models to learn visual token inputs.
Uses a knowledge branch that queries a pathology-specific knowledge graph for morphological features and knowledge tokens.
Evaluated on WSI-Bench, where it reportedly surpasses prior state-of-the-art methods and presents reasoning as intuitive graphs.
Its modular knowledge path is designed to complement vision-aligned MLLMs and support other domains with curated knowledge graphs.
papers.selection_reason: Integrates knowledge graphs into an MLLM for explainable histopathology report generation, fitting Multimodal Foundation Models and Language Foundation Models.
papers.title: PathKGen: Pathology Knowledge Assisted MLLM for Explainable Histopathology
papers.tldr: PathKGen improves explainable histopathology report generation by combining visual pathology features with knowledge-graph-derived reasoning tokens in an MLLM.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning substantially reduces the inference cost of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), yet existing methods are mostly training-free and plug-and-play. They treat the resulting performance drop as an inevitable cost of compression and pursue increasingly complex pruning rules. We rethink this view through two questions: how much of the loss can post-training rescue, and, building on this recovery, how can joint compression push pruning to its limit? We curate a 282K-sample post-training mixture covering general VQA, reasoning, OCR, and grounding, and post-train 36 configurations that drop or merge tokens under a unified protocol. Post-training rescues most of the loss, even for OCR and grounding, and its adaptation gain in closing the gap between the pruned and the dense model grows as the budget tightens. For joint compression, we find that the vision encoder, not the LLM, dominates prefill time in native-resolution MLLMs, so where tokens are removed matters more than how many: keeping 40% of tokens at the encoder runs faster than keeping 10% at the projector. Our best configuration prunes the encoder lightly and the projector aggressively, leaves the LLM intact, and keeps general understanding and reasoning at the dense level. It accelerates the LLM stage by 3.49x but the end-to-end time-to-first-token by only 1.54x, showing that LLM-stage speedups overstate end-to-end gains. We hope these findings offer insights for future research on joint visual token compression. Our data, protocol, and code will be released.
authors: Peiran Yin, Hao Wu, Zihao Yang, Haozhe Hu, Xudong Wang, Xiaoyu Shen
bullets: Post-training largely restores pruning-induced performance loss, including on OCR and grounding tasks.
A 282K-sample mixture spanning VQA, reasoning, OCR, and grounding supports a unified evaluation of 36 compression configurations.
In native-resolution MLLMs, the vision encoder dominates prefill time, making encoder-side pruning more impactful than projector-side pruning.
The best setup lightly prunes the encoder, aggressively prunes the projector, and keeps the LLM unchanged while preserving general understanding and reasoning at dense-model levels.
A 3.49× LLM-stage speedup translates to only a 1.54× end-to-end time-to-first-token improvement.
papers.selection_reason: Rethinks visual token pruning in MLLMs, introducing post-training recovery and joint compression strategies, fitting Efficient AI and Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: Rescuing Your Pruning: Rethinking Visual Token Pruning and Post-Training Recovery in MLLMs
papers.tldr: Post-training can recover most of the accuracy lost to visual token pruning, while pruning location—not just token count—is critical for end-to-end MLLM speed.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are bottlenecked by the scarcity of robot data. Egocentric human manipulation videos offer an abundant, diverse, and semantically-rich alternative that inherently captures manipulation intent. However, the embodiment gap makes it difficult to extract action-relevant representations from these videos. From the perspective of action execution, human hands and robots share analogous manipulation primitives---reaching, grasping, placing---yet exhibit distinct kinematics tied to their embodiments. This might motivate our key approach: egocentric video pretraining can yield shared action representations capturing transferable manipulation skills, while human-specific motion patterns should be disentangled to avoid interfering with robot policy learning. To this end, we propose EXE, an Egocentric Cross(X)-Embodiment pretraining framework that learns a factorized latent action representation from egocentric human videos, separating shared manipulation priors from embodiment-specific signals. By leveraging the shared action space, the robot policy acquires generalizable manipulation semantics from diverse human demonstrations without being biased by human-specific kinematics. This shared knowledge transfers across embodiments with different kinematic structures, enabling the same pretraining to benefit both parallel grippers and dexterous hands. EXE yields consistent gains over baseline without pretraining on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa GR1, and real-world manipulation tasks.
authors: Qingyuan Cai, Bo Zhang, Yongzhen Huang, Jianyu Chen
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of robot data and the human–robot embodiment gap.
Learns factorized latent actions that disentangle shared manipulation primitives from embodiment-specific signals.
Transfers manipulation semantics from diverse human demonstrations to robots with different kinematic structures.
Supports both parallel grippers and dexterous hands.
Reports consistent gains over no-pretraining baselines on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa GR1, and real-world manipulation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Pretrains VLA models from egocentric human videos using factorized latent actions; directly relevant to embodied learning and latent action models.
papers.title: EXE: Egocentric Cross-Embodiment Pretraining via Factorized Latent Actions for VLA Models
papers.tldr: EXE pretrains VLA models on egocentric human videos by separating transferable manipulation skills from human-specific motion, improving robot control across embodiments.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing a coherent 3D scene from uncurated image collections remains challenging due to the presence of irrelevant or non-overlapping views. Recent work has shown that feed-forward reconstruction models contain internal view-consistency signals that support distractor rejection. However, reference-conditioned filtering relies on a curated clean reference, which is not guaranteed in practical image collections.
