To address this limitation, we introduce FreeView, a training-free framework that jointly selects a filtering reference and rejects distractor views from an uncurated collection. FreeView leverages collection-level consensus to identify a representative view that serves as a reliable reference for filtering. It then adapts view rejection to each input collection by combining complementary visual and geometric evidence. This approach preserves useful views under substantial appearance and viewpoint variations while rejecting distractors. FreeView integrates with both VGGT and pi^3, removing the need for a manually curated reference or manual calibration of view rejection. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate high clean-view retention and distractor rejection rates, leading to reliable 3D reconstruction from uncurated views.
authors: Junho Kim, Hyunyoung Choi, Seongwon Lee
bullets: Addresses irrelevant and non-overlapping views that can disrupt reconstruction.
Uses collection-level consensus to select a representative filtering reference.
Combines visual and geometric evidence to adapt view rejection to each collection.
Integrates with VGGT and pi^3 while preserving useful views under appearance and viewpoint variation.
Experiments across multiple datasets show high clean-view retention and distractor rejection, improving reconstruction reliability.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces FreeView for 3D reconstruction from uncurated views by jointly selecting a reference and rejecting distractors, fitting 3D Vision.
papers.title: FreeView: Robust 3D Reconstruction from Uncurated Views
papers.tldr: FreeView enables reliable 3D reconstruction from uncurated image collections by automatically choosing a reference view and rejecting distractors without training or manual calibration.

papers.abstract: GUI grounding requires locating small controls in cluttered screenshots and identifying which control a natural-language instruction refers to. Cropping and enlargement can expose local detail, but the resulting image may still leave ambiguity about the intended target. We propose PreView, an auxiliary preprocessor that improves the inputs to an existing grounding model without further training that model. PreView prepares two complementary types of input features: task-relevant views for localization and candidate-specific cues for target understanding. A trained lightweight auxiliary model predicts and refines a center, crops the screenshot into a local view, and enlarges that view for zoomed-in grounding. It also prepares a visual cue (i.e., a red-circle marker with a location hint) and a textual cue describing the candidate's identity or function. The frozen grounding model uses the prepared inputs to predict the final click. Across five benchmarks, PreView improves the average grounding accuracy of Qwen3-VL-2B, OS-Atlas-4B, and Qwen3-VL-4B without further training these grounding models. Extensive analyses examine the contributions of views and cues, center refinement, and visual input budgets.
authors: Wenjun Hou, Kaishuai Xu
bullets: Targets the difficulty of locating small, ambiguous controls in cluttered GUI screenshots.
Uses a lightweight trained auxiliary model to predict and refine a target center, then crop and enlarge a local view.
Adds candidate-specific cues: a red-circle location marker and text describing the candidate’s identity or function.
Improves average grounding accuracy across five benchmarks for Qwen3-VL-2B, OS-Atlas-4B, and Qwen3-VL-4B without retraining them.
Analyses assess the roles of views, cues, center refinement, and visual input budgets.
papers.selection_reason: Improves GUI grounding for VLMs (Qwen3-VL) using an auxiliary preprocessor that generates task-relevant views and cues, fitting Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: PreView: Enhancing GUI Grounding with Preprocessed Views and Cues
papers.tldr: PreView improves GUI grounding by preprocessing screenshots into localized views and candidate-specific visual/textual cues for a frozen grounding model.

papers.abstract: Attribute-based person retrieval ranks surveillance images from a binary query of semantic attributes, but mean Average Attribute Degree of Match (mADM) drops on unseen cameras as predicted probabilities shift. Common pipelines rank gallery images by their L1 distance to the query, which penalizes a confident single-attribute mismatch no more than small uncertainties across many attributes, while post-hoc recalibration fitted on source validation data fails to transfer because the per-attribute maps fitted on source data do not match those of new cameras. We propose LENS (Likelihood Evaluation and Neighbor Smoothing), combining fine-tuned DINOv3 and CLIP models with a distilled student. LENS regularizes mutually exclusive attribute groups with group cross-entropy in training, scores gallery images by the log-likelihood of the exact query, and smooths gallery logits over nearest neighbors using DINOv3 appearance features from the same forward pass. On held-out datasets, all three changes raise mADM: the likelihood score improves all six retrieval metrics for the main ensemble and mADM for all 48 development models, and training-free kNN smoothing improves all 46 tested development models. On the hidden test set of the UPAR 2027 benchmark, LENS reaches 68.17 mADM.
authors: Nguyen Dang Duy Tan, Vo Thanh Nguyen, Linh T. T. Tran, Huynh Nguyen Phat
bullets: Addresses mADM degradation caused by probability shifts across unseen cameras and limitations of L1-distance ranking.
Uses fine-tuned DINOv3 and CLIP models with a distilled student, plus group cross-entropy for mutually exclusive attributes.
Ranks gallery images by the exact query’s log-likelihood rather than L1 distance.
Smooths gallery logits over appearance-based nearest neighbors using DINOv3 features from the same forward pass.
All evaluated changes improve reported development metrics; LENS achieves 68.17 mADM on the UPAR 2027 hidden test set.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses domain shift in person retrieval using DINOv3 and CLIP, introducing likelihood evaluation and neighbor smoothing, fitting Multimodal Foundation Models and Adaptation and Memory.
papers.title: LENS: Likelihood Evaluation and Neighbor Smoothing for Attribute-Based Person Retrieval on Unseen Cameras
papers.tldr: LENS improves attribute-based person retrieval on unseen cameras by combining likelihood-based ranking, group-aware training, and neighbor smoothing.

papers.abstract: Pedestrian Attribute Recognition (PAR) predicts semantic attributes of individuals, such as gender, age, clothing and accessories, and its descriptions support attribute-based person retrieval and person re-identification. However, accurately recognizing fine-grained attributes across domains remains challenging due to occlusion, appearance variations, and shifts in image distributions. Ensembles of independently trained foundation encoders combine their logits with fixed fusion weights, so every attribute uses the same mix and the encoders are never trained together. We propose UniQuery, which instead jointly fine-tunes DINOv3 and CLIP for attribute-specific fusion. It combines two query heads, one for each encoder, with a joint query head whose attribute queries attend to tokens from both encoders, and the prediction is the average of the logits of the three query heads. We evaluate UniQuery on the benchmark of the UPAR Challenge 2027 at the WACV 2027 Real-World Surveillance workshop, where models are trained on PA100k, PETA and Market-1501 with a shared set of attributes. In leave-one-dataset-out experiments, UniQuery outperforms the independent ensemble in Challenge_Avg on both held-out datasets. Ablations show that learning fusion over independently trained encoders does not improve upon logit averaging in the mean over the two held-out datasets, while freezing the encoders lowers the Challenge_Avg of UniQuery. On the hidden test set of the benchmark, UniQuery achieves a Challenge_Avg of 0.8001.
authors: Nguyen Dang Duy Tan, Linh T. T. Tran, Huynh Nguyen Phat, Vo Thanh Nguyen
bullets: Targets fine-grained pedestrian attributes under occlusion, appearance variation, and domain shift.
Uses separate query heads for DINOv3 and CLIP plus a joint head whose queries attend to both encoders’ tokens.
Averages logits from the three heads for final attribute predictions.
Outperforms an independently trained ensemble in leave-one-dataset-out Challenge_Avg evaluations.
Achieves a Challenge_Avg of 0.8001 on the benchmark’s hidden test set; freezing encoders reduces performance.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes UniQuery to unify DINOv3 and CLIP for cross-domain pedestrian attribute recognition, focusing on joint query heads and fusion strategies for foundation encoders.
papers.title: UniQuery: Unifying Vision Models with a Joint Query Head for Cross-Domain Pedestrian Attribute Recognition
papers.tldr: UniQuery jointly fine-tunes DINOv3 and CLIP with attribute-specific query-based fusion to improve cross-domain pedestrian attribute recognition.

papers.abstract: Pavement crack segmentation under low light is degraded by reduced contrast, shadows, headlight glare, joints, stains, and wet seams. Existing crack segmentation methods mostly assume good illumination. Low-light enhancement methods improve visual quality, but they do not explicitly preserve crack topology. To address these limitations, we formulate low-light crack segmentation as a degradation-aware, prompt-grounded structural defect segmentation problem and propose DROA-CLIPSeg, a parameter-efficient framework that adapts a frozen CLIPSeg vision language backbone using two lightweight modules. QKV Low-Rank Adaptation is injected into the Q/K/V projections of the vision and text encoders to improve crack-specific image text alignment without backbone fine-tuning. The proposed Domain Residual Orthogonal Adapter (DROA) decomposes intermediate features into a dominant crack-domain branch, which captures recurring low-light crack patterns, and an orthogonal residual branch, which preserves faint, thin, and fragmented evidence usually suppressed by noise, shadow, or over-smoothing. We also introduce CrackLingo-9K and CrackLingo-12K, text augmented versions of Crack9k and Crack12k with crack-aware prompts. Training only approximately 1.93 M parameters, corresponding to 1.3% of the full model, DROA-CLIPSeg outperforms 9 zero-shot and 4 fine-tuned vision language baselines on both splits, generalises zero-shot to MVTec AD across textures and defect morphologies, and is supported by extensive ablations. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/VShuklacode/DROA-CLIPSeg
authors: Vinita Shukla, Partibha Jangra, Vinayak Pathak, Praful Hambarde, Amit Shukla
bullets: Addresses low contrast, shadows, glare, stains, joints, and wet seams that impair conventional crack segmentation.
Uses QKV low-rank adaptation to improve crack-specific image–text alignment without fine-tuning the backbone.
Introduces a Domain Residual Orthogonal Adapter that separates dominant crack patterns from residual faint, thin, and fragmented evidence.
Provides CrackLingo-9K and CrackLingo-12K, prompt-augmented versions of existing crack datasets.
Reports better performance than 9 zero-shot and 4 fine-tuned vision-language baselines, with zero-shot generalization to MVTec AD; results are limited to the evaluated datasets and settings.
papers.selection_reason: Adapts CLIPSeg for low-light crack segmentation using parameter-efficient adapters (QKV Low-Rank Adaptation, DROA), fitting Multimodal Foundation Models and Efficient AI.
papers.title: DROA-CLIPSeg: Prompt-Guided Thin Crack Segmentation in Low-Light Conditions
papers.tldr: DROA-CLIPSeg enables thin pavement-crack segmentation in low-light imagery by adapting a frozen CLIPSeg model with lightweight, crack-aware modules that preserve faint structural evidence.

papers.abstract: While interactive video world models require autoregressive generation, directly adapting pretrained bidirectional video diffusion models into autoregressive ones with teacher forcing can disrupt their visual priors and degrade autoregressive generation quality. In this paper, we introduce Mix Forcing, a causal pre-training paradigm for interactive video world models, implemented with the Mixture-of-Bidirectional-and-Autoregressive (MoBA) attention. Mix Forcing jointly trains a video diffusion model with both teacher forcing and bidirectional training, yielding a strong causal initialization for few-step post-training. In self-attention, Mix Forcing leverages teacher forcing to learn causal next-chunk prediction for autoregressive rollout, while using bidirectional attention to preserve pretrained visual priors. To support online text interaction, Mix Forcing further adopts a chunk-wise cross-attention design that conditions each video chunk on a shared environment prompt and its own local prompt, without exposing future instructions to the current chunk. Following causal pre-training on a 14B image-to-video model, we apply consistency and distribution matching distillation to obtain a four-step autoregressive generator. Experiments on our internal benchmark and public benchmarks, including WBench and SANA-WM-Bench, show that our model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with precise camera control. Notably, our model supports high-fidelity long-horizon generation without quality degradation even over one-hour rollouts. Project page is here: https://zelingao98.github.io/mixforcing
authors: Zelin Gao, Hao Ouyang, Jiapeng Zhu, Qiuyu Wang, Jingye Chen, Zichen Liu, Xing Zhu, Yujun Shen, Yinghao Xu
bullets: Addresses the degradation of visual priors when adapting bidirectional video diffusion models to causal, autoregressive generation.
Introduces MoBA attention, jointly combining teacher-forced causal prediction with bidirectional training for causal initialization.
Uses chunk-wise cross-attention to condition video on shared environment context and local instructions without revealing future prompts.
Applies consistency and distribution-matching distillation to produce a four-step autoregressive generator.
Reports state-of-the-art visual quality, event following, and camera control, with high-fidelity rollouts lasting up to one hour on reported benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Causal pre-training with mixture attention for interactive video world models, enabling long-horizon autoregressive rollout.
papers.title: Mix Forcing: Causal Pre-Training via Mixture Attention for Interactive World Models
papers.tldr: Mix Forcing converts bidirectional video diffusion models into efficient autoregressive world models while preserving visual quality and enabling long-horizon interactive generation.

papers.abstract: Cooperative transport with heterogeneous legged robots requires coordinating different motion capabilities while supporting an unfixed shared payload. We present HA-DiPO (Heterogeneous-Agent Diffusion Policy Optimization), a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework under centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE). The framework decouples team-level coordination from embodiment-specific motion control: at the high level, a centralized critic uses team-value estimates to jointly train independent coordination policies, aligning robot-specific action responses with a shared transport objective; at the low level, embodiment-specific robust motion policies track the coordination commands. The high-level diffusion policies offer more flexible action distributions than single-Gaussian parameterizations, allowing potentially multimodal coordination responses to be represented. The coordination policies learn from scratch through reward-driven simulator interaction without demonstrations. At execution, each robot generates coordination commands using only local robot and payload observations, without partner-state inputs or inter-robot messages. Simulation comparisons show that HA-DiPO achieves higher final mean returns and velocity-tracking success rates, as well as lower velocity errors, than the evaluated baselines. Real-world experiments further demonstrate quadrupedal-wheeled-legged and human-robot cooperative transport.
authors: Xuebin Li, Jinpeng Xiao, Zong Chen, Pierluigi Arpenti, Bruno Siciliano, Jiebao Sun, Yiqun Li
bullets: Targets coordination across robots with different motion capabilities and a shared, unfixed payload.
Uses hierarchical CTDE: a centralized critic trains high-level coordination policies, while embodiment-specific low-level controllers execute commands.
Diffusion policies represent flexible, potentially multimodal coordination responses beyond single-Gaussian policies.
Robots act from local robot and payload observations without partner-state inputs or inter-robot communication.

Simulations report higher mean returns and velocity-tracking success, with lower velocity errors than evaluated baselines; real-world tests include quadrupedal-wheeled-legged and human-robot transport.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning with diffusion policies for heterogeneous cooperative robot transport.
papers.title: HA-DiPO: Diffusion Policy Optimization for Heterogeneous Cooperative Transport
papers.tldr: HA-DiPO enables heterogeneous robots to cooperatively transport an unfixed payload using decentralized diffusion policies trained with centralized critics.

papers.abstract: Simulation provides a low-cost sandbox where embodied agents can attempt tasks, observe outcomes, and learn from experience. Running many diverse simulation environments concurrently can consume substantial CPU and GPU memory because independently constructed scenes duplicate resources that remain unchanged across instances. We present Patchwork, a resource-sharing system for domain-randomized simulation, built around the representation $E=T+\Delta$: a shared template contains common resources, and a patch records the mutations needed to construct a target environment. Patchwork separates randomization sampling from replay and selects reusable templates together with patches that preserve each target environment's intended configuration. Its layered runtime shares compiled model structure and immutable assets while keeping mutable parameters and simulation state private to each instance. We implement Patchwork on robosuite and MuJoCo and evaluate it on LIBERO-plus and RoboCasa365 workloads. At 32 replicas, shared-template execution reduces CPU RSS by 88-92% relative to process-per-environment execution. Controlled experiments show how sharing shifts memory growth toward template diversity and unique asset content rather than instance count, within the supported sharing boundaries.
authors: Zixu Hao, Weijun Wang, Xiangyu Li, Liang Mi, Hao Wu, Yunxin Liu, Ting Cao
bullets: Addresses duplicated CPU and GPU memory from independently constructed simulation scenes.
Represents each environment as a shared template plus a mutation patch: E = T + Δ.
Separates randomization sampling from replay and keeps mutable parameters and simulation state private.
Implemented with robosuite and MuJoCo, evaluated on LIBERO-plus and RoboCasa365 workloads.
At 32 replicas, reduces CPU RSS by 88–92%; memory growth depends more on template diversity and unique assets than replica count within supported boundaries.
papers.selection_reason: Resource-sharing system reducing memory for domain-randomized embodied simulation, a technically transferable efficiency contribution to AI training pipelines.
papers.title: Replicate What Varies: Resource Sharing for Domain-Randomized Embodied Simulation
papers.tldr: Patchwork reduces the memory cost of running many domain-randomized embodied simulations by sharing reusable resources while preserving per-environment changes and state.

papers.abstract: Megapixel visual synthesis with latent diffusion models requires operating far beyond the resolutions at which these models are typically trained. Cascade refinement is a leading strategy for this setting: it starts from a base image at a native resolution and progressively upsamples it to the target resolution through multiple refinement stages. Each stage typically performs a pixel-space resolution transition followed by latent-space denoising. While prior acceleration efforts mainly focus on reducing denoising cost, we identify a complementary and underexplored bottleneck: the repeated movement of representations through the VAE. We call these operations pixel-space transitions. In cascade pipelines, intermediate latents are often decoded to RGB, resized, and re-encoded before refinement, while final latents are decoded patch by patch with dense overlap to suppress boundary artifacts. We propose UltraFlash, a transition-efficient approach that accelerates these VAE-heavy operations. UltraFlash has two components. Latent Hyperloop replaces intermediate RGB round trips with a learned latent-space shortcut that approximates the decode-resize-encode transformation without repeated VAE decoding and encoding. Sparse Patch-based Decoding accelerates final reconstruction by addressing patch seams caused by inconsistent GroupNorm statistics and reusing cached statistics across patches, enabling sparse VAE decoding with much smaller overlap. Integrated into a state-of-the-art cascade baseline, UltraFlash reduces 4K generation latency by approximately 2x while improving image quality. These results show that optimizing pixel-space transitions can improve both efficiency and fidelity, offering an effective route toward fast, high-quality megapixel visual synthesis.
authors: Phuc Lai, Anh Nguyen, Phong Nguyen, Anh Tran
bullets: Targets an underexplored bottleneck in cascade refinement: repeated decoding, resizing, and re-encoding through the VAE.
Latent Hyperloop replaces intermediate RGB round trips with a learned latent-space approximation.
Sparse Patch-based Decoding reduces overlap between final reconstruction patches by reusing GroupNorm statistics, mitigating seams.
Integrated into a cascade baseline, UltraFlash approximately halves 4K generation latency and improves quality.
Focuses on VAE-heavy pixel-space transitions rather than only reducing denoising cost.
papers.selection_reason: Reduces latency of VAE-heavy cascade visual synthesis; efficiency contribution to generative pipelines.
papers.title: UltraFlash: Accelerating Megapixel Visual Synthesis
papers.tldr: UltraFlash accelerates 4K latent-diffusion image synthesis by reducing costly VAE-based resolution transitions while improving image quality.

papers.abstract: Running a language model and a dense 3D map on one device means the two share one memory, and exceeding its limit is an out-of-memory failure. Map systems that keep a bounded working set bound it by a count of keyframes, but the memory one keyframe occupies varies widely with what it carries, so a count does not control what the working set occupies. The unit of admission is as poorly matched, since a radius around the pose, a fixed cell, or the graph neighbors of the last matched keyframe all move parts of the map that are not needed. We therefore propose two decisions. First, the memory the resident map uses is bounded directly, and the cost of every admission is known before any data is read, from per-keyframe resident sizes computed offline and carried with the map. Second, keyframes are admitted and released at a semantic spatial unit, the rooms and corridors of the building, so that the robot holds the zone it occupies together with the zone it is about to enter while the zones it has passed are released. Every admission measures the resident total, makes room, and only then reads, so the budget is never overshot. On two NVIDIA Jetson boards the budget holds in every run and the model gives up at most 0.8 percent of its throughput, whereas without it the operating system kills the model or the map. Under that budget, and over the environments evaluated, admission by semantic zone localizes 6-9 points more of the query frames than a geometric partition of matched zone count and about twice as much as the retrieval of RTAB-Map, at a lower ATE. Bounding memory lets the map and the model coexist, and moving the map in semantic zones makes the bounded map usable.
authors: Huichang Yun, Jaeyeul Kim, Seungho Yoo
bullets: Keyframe-count limits are unreliable because keyframes vary substantially in memory usage.
The system predicts each keyframe’s resident size offline and enforces a strict memory budget before reading new data.
It admits and releases map content by rooms and corridors, retaining the current and next zones while removing passed zones.
On two NVIDIA Jetson boards, the budget held in every run with at most 0.8% model-throughput loss.
Semantic-zone admission localized 6–9 percentage points more query frames than geometric partitioning and about twice as much as RTAB-Map retrieval, with lower ATE in the evaluated environments.
papers.selection_reason: Memory-bounded keyframe management for dense maps on robots, a form of embodied spatial memory.
papers.title: Memory-Aware Keyframe Management for Dense Maps on Memory-Constrained Robots
papers.tldr: A memory-aware map manager enables language models and dense 3D maps to coexist on constrained robots by budgeting memory directly and loading semantic spatial zones on demand.

papers.abstract: Video world models are expected to generate videos that accurately follow specified camera trajectories while maintaining consistent 3D structures. However, existing models are predominantly trained on densely sampled videos with small inter-frame camera motions. When applied to sparse, large step trajectories, they often produce frozen frames, inaccurate camera motion, and severe geometric drift. We attribute this degradation to a mismatch between the gradual viewpoint transitions seen during training and the large viewpoint changes required at inference time. To address this problem, we propose Dense Trajectory Teacher Distillation (DTTD), a post-training framework that transfers a model's generation capability from dense trajectories to large camera motions. Given a sparse trajectory, DTTD interpolates additional camera poses to construct a dense trajectory covering the same path. The frozen base model then generates reliable teacher videos along this familiar dense trajectory, and pose aligned teacher observations are used to evaluate candidate videos generated under the original sparse trajectory. In this way, the model serves as its own generation teacher, requiring neither additional video data nor a stronger external video generator. We further combine dense teacher supervision with geometry aware rewards that assess cross frame consistency and camera trajectory following, and use the resulting preferences for offline preference optimization. To stably expand the model's motion range, we introduce a cumulative curriculum that progressively incorporates larger motion steps while retaining simpler trajectories to reduce capability forgetting.
authors: Shuofeng Sun, Linqing Zhao, Haibin Yan
bullets: Existing models often fail on sparse, large-step camera trajectories, producing frozen frames, inaccurate motion, and geometric drift.
DTTD interpolates sparse camera paths into dense trajectories that the frozen base model can reliably generate.
Pose-aligned dense teacher videos supervise candidate outputs generated on the original sparse trajectory, without extra data or an external teacher.
Geometry-aware rewards measure cross-frame consistency and trajectory following for offline preference optimization.
A cumulative curriculum progressively increases motion difficulty while retaining simpler trajectories to limit capability forgetting.
papers.selection_reason: Post-training framework to extend video world models to large camera motions via dense teacher distillation.
papers.title: Distilling Dense Trajectory Teachers For Large-Motion Video World Models
papers.tldr: DTTD extends video world models from small to large camera motions by using dense-trajectory self-teaching, geometry-aware rewards, and curriculum-based preference optimization.

papers.abstract: Robot policy evaluation informs deployment decisions and policy improvement, but physical testing and simulator preparation require substantial effort. World models offer a complementary route through closed-loop interaction in generated environments. Recent benchmarks have demonstrated their potential as policy evaluators through outcome-based evaluation (i.e., assessing task success or failure). However, such evaluation does not establish whether world models faithfully simulate how policies fail. Misrepresenting failures can lead to incorrect diagnoses of policy weaknesses and make policies appear ready for deployment even when small scene changes cause them to fail. We therefore ask: do world models faithfully simulate how and at which stages policies fail, and under what conditions they transition from success to failure? To answer this question, we introduce WorldFailBench with three evaluation tasks. Failure reason tests whether models reproduce the observable errors policies make. Failure stage assesses whether failures concentrate at the same stages of full-task execution. Failure boundary examines whether models reproduce the conditions under which policies transition from success to failure under controlled scene changes in simulation. The benchmark covers manipulation tasks in the LIBERO and RoboTwin simulation environments and real-world manipulation tasks performed by the G1 humanoid robot. Experiments across seven world models reveal substantial gaps in their understanding of policy failures, providing guidance for developing more reliable world models for policy evaluation.
authors: Zheng Zhang, Xiaoyang Tang, Shuaiqi Cheng, Jiakai Huang, Zhongbo Wu, Ziyi Zhang, Yuan Si, Zeyu Liu, Weibo Gao, Shunyu Liu, Shan You, Fei Wang, Xiaogang Wang, Dacheng Tao
bullets: Introduces three failure-focused evaluation tasks: failure reason, failure stage, and failure boundary.
Tests manipulation policies in LIBERO, RoboTwin, and real-world G1 humanoid robot tasks.
Evaluates seven world models for closed-loop policy evaluation.
Finds substantial gaps in world models’ ability to understand and simulate policy failures.
Highlights the need for more reliable world models before using them to guide deployment decisions.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark evaluating whether world models faithfully simulate policy failures in closed-loop interaction.
papers.title: WorldFailBench: Do World Models Understand Policy Failures?
papers.tldr: WorldFailBench evaluates whether world models faithfully reproduce not just policy outcomes, but also the reasons, stages, and conditions of robot policy failures.

papers.abstract: Video spatial reasoning requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to understand how objects are arranged and related across viewpoints. While these models can recognize objects in individual frames, integrating these observations to solve complex spatial tasks remains challenging. We examine route planning as a representative task and observe that existing models become substantially less accurate as the number of required turns increases, with several models achieving accuracy close to random guessing on routes requiring three or more turns. This finding suggests that recognizing landmarks alone is insufficient: models must also connect observations across viewpoints and track how landmarks are arranged in a shared space. Motivated by this observation, we introduce GeoLift, a training-free framework that uses feed-forward 3D reconstruction to map objects detected in individual frames into a shared metric 3D scene. GeoLift combines a frozen MLLM for 2D grounding with pretrained geometry models for scene reconstruction. It then uses shared geometric regions, called superpoints, to associate observations of the same object across views without a learned matcher. The reconstructed 3D map enables explicit computation of spatial relations and multistep routes, and provides geometric evidence for estimating distances and sizes. With all model weights frozen, GeoLift improves Qwen3-VL-4B's average score on VSI-Bench from 55.4% to 64.1%, including an increase in route-planning accuracy from 30.9% to 53.6%, and achieves 59.8% accuracy on MindCube. These results show that connecting frame-level object grounding through a shared 3D map can improve complex spatial reasoning without task-specific training.
authors: Xinglin Li, TingTing Long, Jingzhi Zhou, Jiajing Chen, Jian Yang, Jin Xie
bullets: Existing MLLMs struggle to connect landmarks across viewpoints, with accuracy dropping sharply on routes requiring three or more turns.
GeoLift combines a frozen MLLM for 2D grounding with pretrained feed-forward geometry models for training-free 3D reconstruction.
Shared geometric regions called superpoints associate the same objects across views without a learned matcher.
The resulting 3D map supports explicit spatial-relation and multistep-route computation, plus distance and size estimation.
It raises Qwen3-VL-4B’s VSI-Bench average from 55.4% to 64.1% and route-planning accuracy from 30.9% to 53.6%, while reaching 59.8% on MindCube.
papers.selection_reason: Grounds video spatial reasoning in explicit 3D maps, improving MLLM spatial and route reasoning.
papers.title: GeoLift: Grounding Video Spatial Reasoning in Explicit 3D Maps
papers.tldr: GeoLift improves video spatial reasoning by mapping frame-level object detections into an explicit shared 3D scene for multiview route planning and spatial inference.

papers.abstract: High-resolution remote sensing (RS) imagery provides fine spatial detail over large areas, making it essential for fine-grained scene understanding. Referring Remote Sensing Image Segmentation (RRSIS) aims to segment regions described by natural language, yet many existing methods rely on sequential alignment--fusion pipelines with limited joint modeling of cross-scale visual hierarchies and linguistic dependencies. Moreover, dense attention mechanisms struggle with the sparsity and wide spatial dispersion of RS targets, while current datasets offer limited structured evaluation of multi-target references, multi-hop relational reasoning, and multi-granularity descriptions, limiting both model development and evaluation. To address these challenges, we propose a Cross-Scale Sparse Attention Model (CSSAM), which aligns multiscale visual features with complex referring expressions through two key modules. The Cross-scale Modality-aligned Fusion Module (CMFM) performs unified cross-scale cross-modal fusion, while the Dynamic Multimodal Sparse Hybrid Attention (DMSHA) selectively attends to informative visual--textual tokens, reducing dense visual interactions. Furthermore, we introduce M$^{3}$RRSIS-D, a RRSIS dataset explicitly designed around three core reasoning dimensions: multi-target (M$^{1}$), reference-dependent multi-hop (M$^{2}$), and multi-granularity (M$^{3}$) expressions. Extensive experiments on M$^{3}$RRSIS-D and two public RRSIS benchmarks demonstrate that CSSAM achieves competitive performance across accuracy, fine-grained reasoning, and high-IoU localization metrics, validating its effectiveness for complex semantic reasoning in realistic RS scenarios. Code, dataset, and model weights will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Yuxi Li, Lu Si, Xia Liao, Yidong Shen, Zheng Wei, Jun Zhang, Xin Yuan
bullets: Targets the difficulty of segmenting spatially sparse, widely dispersed regions described by complex natural-language references.
Uses CMFM for unified cross-scale cross-modal fusion and DMSHA to selectively attend to informative visual–textual tokens.
Introduces M³RRSIS-D, covering multi-target, reference-dependent multi-hop, and multi-granularity expressions.
Experiments on the new dataset and two public benchmarks report competitive accuracy, fine-grained reasoning, and high-IoU localization.
Code, data, and model weights are planned for release upon acceptance.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes dynamic multimodal sparse attention to reduce dense visual interactions, fitting efficient attention.
papers.title: Cross-Scale Sparse Attention for Referring Segmentation in Remote Sensing
papers.tldr: CSSAM improves referring segmentation in remote-sensing imagery by jointly fusing multiscale vision and language features with sparse attention, supported by a new reasoning-focused dataset.

papers.abstract: Recent vision-and-language navigation (VLN) policies act on their visual history, and an incorrect action can take them off the instructed route. Paired interventions on four VLN policies show that clearing the history doubles pooled success at the onset of a deviation but lowers it on route, while later in a deviation, removing only the off-route frames helps much less. After a deviation, the retained history keeps the policy from turning where a turn is needed, which we call behavioral inertia. We propose MOON, a framework that equips a frozen VLN policy with two lightweight modules, adding less than 1% of its parameters. A deviation judge decides when to forget, raising an alarm that clears the history when it predicts that the agent is off route. A recovery policy, trained with GRPO from alarm states, learns how to move on, turning more of the successes found only by sampling into a single greedy rollout. Experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE show that MOON reaches the highest R2R-CE success rate among the compared methods and raises the success rate of its frozen base by 5.2 and 6.0 points, and an ablation with a random trigger indicates that this gain depends on when the history is cleared. Without retraining, MOON also improves zero-shot object-goal navigation on HM3D-OVON. Together, these results suggest that deviation recovery depends on knowing when to forget, not only how to act. Code is available at https://github.com/AutoLab-SAI-SJTU/MOON.
authors: Jingmeng Zhou, Seson Sun, Binyao Xu, Lingming Zhang, Hanshi Wang, Fudong Ge, Weiming Hu, Jin Gao, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Incorrect actions can create behavioral inertia: retained off-route history prevents the agent from turning when needed.
MOON adds two lightweight modules to a frozen VLN policy: a deviation judge that triggers history clearing and a recovery policy trained from alarm states.
On R2R-CE and RxR-CE, MOON improves its frozen base success by 5.2 and 6.0 percentage points, respectively, and achieves the highest R2R-CE success among compared methods.
A random-trigger ablation shows that recovery depends on clearing history at the right time, not merely clearing it.
MOON also improves zero-shot object-goal navigation on HM3D-OVON without retraining.
papers.selection_reason: Vision-and-language navigation with history clearing and recovery, directly addressing embodied navigation memory.
papers.title: MOON: Learning When to Forget and How to Move On in Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: MOON helps vision-and-language navigation agents recover from route deviations by learning when to clear misleading visual history and how to continue afterward.

papers.abstract: Image tokenizers convert pixels into compact latent sequences for efficient generative modeling. Most approaches arrange latents on a downsampled two-dimensional grid, tying sequence length to image resolution. We compare two variable-length strategies: computationally efficient patch-derived tokens, which inherit explicit spatial organization, and more demanding register tokens, which have no predefined spatial layout. Our reconstruction results reveal that patch-derived tokens perform substantially better under extreme compression, whereas register tokens achieve slightly better reconstruction quality at intermediate budgets. At high token budgets, both approaches achieve similar reconstruction quality. For downstream generative tasks, register tokens outperform patch-derived tokens. Adding representation alignment with external pretrained visual encoders substantially improves the generative performance of patch-derived tokens, allowing them to match or outperform register tokens depending on the token budget. We further find that both approaches learn spatially localized representations. Patch-derived tokens largely retain their explicitly imposed spatial organization, while register tokens develop an implicit two-dimensional spatial structure despite having no predefined layout. Representation alignment reduces this spatial organizational constraint, enabling individual tokens to exert a stronger non-local influence.
authors: Philipp Schenkel, Tobias Sch\"urmann, Omer Sahin Tas
bullets: Compares variable-length patch-derived tokens with layout-free register tokens for image tokenization.
Patch-derived tokens are substantially better at extreme compression; register tokens are slightly better at intermediate budgets, and both converge at high budgets.
Register tokens outperform patch-derived tokens in downstream generative tasks without additional alignment.
Aligning representations with pretrained visual encoders improves patch-derived generative performance, sometimes matching or surpassing register tokens.
Both token types develop spatially localized representations; alignment weakens this spatial constraint and promotes more non-local token influence.
papers.selection_reason: Compares variable-length image tokenizers for compact latent sequences, relevant to efficient generative modeling.
papers.title: Patch-Derived or Register Tokens? Comparing Variable-Length Image Tokenizers
papers.tldr: Patch-derived tokens reconstruct images better under extreme compression, while register tokens excel for generative tasks; representation alignment can close or reverse this gap.

papers.abstract: Skill learning enables web agents to reuse prior experience for long-horizon interactive tasks. However, learned skills are typically evaluated in closed environments, overlooking the fact that real-world web deployment involves continuous shifts in invocation context, perceptual grounding, and execution feasibility. To this end, we introduce SkillShift-Bench, the first benchmark for evaluating skill learning with controlled open-environment shifts. SkillShift-Bench simulates Contextual Shift, Perceptual Shift, and Execution Shift across three self-hosted web systems, and evaluates agents with diagnostics covering task success, interaction cost, skill use, and skill failure. Comprehensive experiments reveal systematic robustness degradation under controlled shifts, characterized by lower success rates, higher interaction costs, and more frequent skill failures, with Execution Shift exerting the strongest pressure. We further formulate shifted skill execution as a nonstationary local executability problem and provide both a dynamic-regret analysis and a practical test-time adaptation method, demonstrating the feasibility of improving learned-skill execution without relearning the skill library. Code, tasks, environments, documentation, and the leaderboard are available at https://skillshift-bench.github.io/.
authors: Bo-Yu Chen, Zhi Zhou, Yu-Feng Li
bullets: Introduces controlled Contextual, Perceptual, and Execution Shifts across three self-hosted web systems.
Measures task success, interaction cost, skill use, and skill failure under changing conditions.
Finds systematic robustness degradation, with Execution Shift producing the strongest impact.
Frames shifted execution as a nonstationary local executability problem and proposes test-time adaptation without relearning the skill library.
Provides code, tasks, environments, documentation, and a leaderboard.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a test-time adaptation method for skill execution under environment shifts, fitting the Test-Time Learning subtopic.
papers.title: SkillShift-Bench: Benchmarking Skill Learning under Environment Evolution for Web Agents
papers.tldr: SkillShift-Bench evaluates how robustly web agents reuse learned skills when deployment environments evolve.

papers.abstract: Running deep models for medical image analysis at the point of care is challenging with standard architectures: convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are often too heavy for edge devices, while Vision Transformers (ViTs) require massive training datasets to compensate for missing inductive biases. This study investigates how far the dual-token distillation used to train data-efficient ViTs can be pushed when applied across architectures, from a CNN-based teacher into a lightweight ViT student. LiteMed-ViT is introduced as a dual-token ViT featuring a convolutional stem and a class-balanced distillation objective; at 0.234M parameters, LiteMed-ViT carries 47.8x fewer parameters than its ResNet18 teacher at a memory footprint of just 0.89 MB. Evaluated against three compact CNN baselines on three MedMNIST subsets of varying modality and class balance, LiteMed-ViT attains higher accuracy than all three baselines on BloodMNIST (95.05%) and two on PathMNIST (89.15%). Under MedMNIST-C corruptions, it is at least as robust as every compact CNN across all subsets, outperforming them on BloodMNIST and PathMNIST without declining in relative standing as severity increases. Particular attention is devoted to identifying the exact conditions where performance plateaus. On DermaMNIST, LiteMed-ViT's balanced accuracy remains up to 1.9 points below the strongest compact CNNs and does not benefit from higher input resolutions up to 224 pixels, where ResNet18 gains 12.6 points. Stronger teachers do not yield a more accurate student, and overconfident ones lower its DermaMNIST balanced accuracy unless calibrated.
authors: Shuaibu Shehu (SR University), Elijah M. Flomo (SR University), Mohammad Safiya (GITAM University), Anurodh Kumar (SR University), Subodh Kumar (Dr. KNS Memorial Institute of Medical Sciences)
bullets: Uses a CNN teacher to distill knowledge into a lightweight ViT with a convolutional stem and class-balanced dual-token objective.
Has 0.234M parameters and a 0.89 MB memory footprint—47.8× fewer parameters than its ResNet18 teacher.
Outperforms compact CNN baselines on BloodMNIST and some PathMNIST evaluations, while matching or exceeding their corruption robustness.
Performance plateaus on DermaMNIST: balanced accuracy remains up to 1.9 points below the strongest CNNs and does not improve with higher resolution.
Stronger or overconfident teachers do not necessarily improve the student; calibration is important for DermaMNIST.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on a lightweight medical vision transformer with reduced parameters and memory, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: Promise and Limits of Cross-Architecture Knowledge Distillation for Lightweight Medical Vision Transformers (LiteMed-ViT)
papers.tldr: LiteMed-ViT shows that cross-architecture distillation can produce an extremely small, robust medical ViT, though its benefits depend strongly on the task and teacher calibration.

papers.abstract: Humanoid motion trackers reproduce diverse behaviors, but sharing a policy across bodies requires accounting for differences in structure, morphology and dynamics. We present MimicAll, a reinforcement-learning framework for shared whole-body motion tracking across heterogeneous humanoids. A structured embodiment descriptor is encoded into global and joint-aligned conditions, which are combined with observation history and body-matched motion references to predict joint-target offsets. Physics-consistent embodiment randomization, body-calibrated retargeting and heterogeneous simulation support training across 4,096 variants from 16 humanoid families. We introduce a benchmark of 464 bodies across five distribution strata to evaluate motion generalization, within-family embodiment shifts and unseen-family transfer. Controlled ablations show that embodiment information improves motion completion with simple concatenation, while self-attention yields the lowest global position errors. With equal training transitions, shared training achieves 99.4% 30-second success on randomized G1 bodies in 100STYLE, versus 42.9% for a single-body specialist. With Flat-MLP encoding and concatenation, continued training on a motion subset excluding obstacle categories achieves 98.3% and 93.5% 30-second success on 100STYLE for sampled training bodies and out-of-distribution variants within seen families, respectively. On an eight-motion LAFAN1 subset excluding ground and get-up sequences across 464 bodies, mismatched body conditions reduce self-attention's 30-second success from 61.7% to 47.0%, demonstrating a closed-loop benefit from embodiment information.
authors: Jia Li, Lingyun Xu, Yitang Li, Hao Zhao
bullets: Addresses morphology, structure, and dynamics differences that hinder cross-humanoid policy sharing.
Encodes embodiment globally and per joint, combining it with observation history and body-matched motion references to predict joint-target offsets.
Uses physics-consistent embodiment randomization, calibrated retargeting, and heterogeneous simulation across 4,096 variants from 16 humanoid families.
Evaluates generalization on 464 bodies across five distribution strata, including within-family shifts and unseen-family transfer.

Embodiment conditioning substantially improves closed-loop tracking; shared training reaches 99.4% 30-second success on randomized G1 bodies versus 42.9% for a single-body specialist, while self-attention gives the lowest global position errors.
papers.selection_reason: Reinforcement-learning whole-body motion tracking across heterogeneous humanoids with embodiment conditioning.
papers.title: MimicAll: Structured Embodiment Conditioning for Cross-Humanoid Whole-Body Motion Tracking
papers.tldr: MimicAll enables one reinforcement-learning policy to track whole-body motion across diverse humanoid bodies by explicitly conditioning it on structured embodiment information.

papers.abstract: Robots can use historical observations to answer spatiotemporal queries in familiar environments, but the presence of relevant evidence does not imply that existing tools support the operations a task requires. We introduce ReSight, a task-driven self-improving memory system for embodied agents that expands the capabilities for processing and accessing historical observations as task demands arise. ReSight retains keyframes and their spatiotemporal associations, separating observation evidence from extensible derived fields so that stored observations can be reprocessed for new needs. An execution agent and a coding agent share this memory through different interfaces: the former calls registered tools within a bounded online budget, while the latter uses a programmable workspace and a larger exploration budget to inspect evidence, write programs, and acquire models as needed. To realize capability expansion in ReSight, we develop Explore-Distill-Mount (EDM), which identifies capability gaps from execution and exploration records without task reference answers and converts exploration-derived solutions into reusable memory builders, query tools, and skills, extending memory representations and access capabilities as needed. Experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate effective base memory access and capability expansion. With the execution model and online budget held fixed within each benchmark, EDM reduces mean position error on OC-NaVQA from 33.10 m to 24.72 m and improves high-level success on FindingDory from 38.3% to 63.8%. With the tools and skill frozen, success still improves by 28.3 percentage points on FindingDory episodes excluded from exploration and distillation. Experiments on real robot patrol memories further demonstrate reuse of these capabilities for subsequent queries and new memories, with fewer online tool calls on average.
authors: Lirong Che, Yang Chen, Yimeng Su, Daqi Liu, Zhenyu Huang, Jiong Wang, Yuzhe Yang, Xu Cao, Chuang Wang, Jian Su, Xueqian Wang
bullets: Addresses the gap between available historical evidence and tools capable of performing task-specific operations.
Stores keyframes and spatiotemporal links separately from extensible derived fields, allowing observations to be reprocessed.
Uses distinct execution and coding agents for bounded online querying versus broader exploration and program/model development.
Its Explore-Distill-Mount process converts discovered solutions into reusable memory builders, query tools, and skills without task reference answers.
Across benchmarks, it reduces OC-NaVQA mean position error from 33.10 m to 24.72 m and raises FindingDory success from 38.3% to 63.8%; real-robot patrol tests show reuse with fewer online tool calls.
papers.selection_reason: Embodied memory system for robots, fitting embodied AI and embodied memory.
papers.title: ReSight: Task-Driven Self-Improving Memory for Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: ReSight enables embodied agents to expand how they process and query historical observations as new task needs arise, improving spatial reasoning and task success.

papers.abstract: Text-to-3D solid retrieval requires aligning natural language with precise geometry despite variations in pose, scale, and recording conventions. Existing methods discretize Boundary Representation (B-rep) models into point clouds or meshes, or learn features from faces, edges, and topology, risking information loss or lacking explicit invariance guarantees. We propose a text-to-B-rep retrieval framework based on group actions and spectral geometric invariants, making invariance an explicit constraint on descriptor construction. Specifically, we use group actions to characterize equivalence transformations induced by translation, rotation, reflection, uniform scaling, and contour recording conventions. For sketch-extrusion solids, we construct a fixed 280-dimensional spectral geometric descriptor by integrating geometric information from three complementary levels, including cross-sectional regions, contour boundaries, and extrusion structures. Furthermore, we use descriptor-consistent multi-positive sets and geometric attribute supervision to promote structural alignment between text and solids. On Text-to-3D solid retrieval, our method achieves 88.6% Recall@5, exceeding the previous state of the art by 13.6 percentage points and demonstrating the effectiveness of explicit geometric invariants for precise 3D solid retrieval.
authors: Hongzhu Yi, Hao Liu, Tao Yu, Tiankun Yang, Yujia Yang, Zhenghao Zhang, Tianyu Zong, Zhenyu Guan, Bingkang Shi, Haopeng Jin, Yuanxiang Wang, Zhongtian Luo, Jungang Xu
bullets: Targets information loss and missing invariance guarantees in point-cloud, mesh, and component-based B-rep representations.
Defines equivalence transformations through group actions, covering translation, rotation, reflection, uniform scaling, and contour conventions.
Builds a fixed 280-dimensional descriptor from cross-sectional regions, contour boundaries, and extrusion structures.
Uses descriptor-consistent multi-positive sets and geometric attribute supervision to improve text–solid structural alignment.
Achieves 88.6% Recall@5, reported as 13.6 percentage points above the previous state of the art.
papers.selection_reason: Text-to-3D retrieval with explicit spectral geometric invariants is directly relevant to spatial and geometric reasoning.
papers.title: Can One Hear Geometry? Gauge-Invariant Spectral Descriptors for Text-to-B-rep Retrieval
papers.tldr: A text-to-B-rep retrieval framework uses explicit spectral geometric invariants to match language with 3D solids despite pose, scale, reflection, and recording variations.

papers.abstract: Lung tumor segmentation plays a vital role in early detection and treatment planning of lung cancer. Although state-of-the-art deep learning models achieve high dice score coefficients (DSC), each forward pass requires computing large amounts of floating point operations, making them computationally expensive, requiring GPU acceleration, and having slow inference speed, limiting real-world clinical deployment. We propose a lightweight, energy-efficient model that leverages the ENet architecture for its real-time inference capability and low computational cost, enhanced with UNet-style skip connections between encoder and decoder stages for feature reuse and the lightweight Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for improved feature representation. The model is trained on publicly available data from The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA) via the Medical Segmentation Decathlon Challenge (MSD) and evaluated on the Lung Image Database Consortium and Image Database Resource Initiative (LIDC-IDRI) dataset. Our model achieves a DSC of 0.90812 (threshold of 0.5) with its compact architecture of 430,052 parameters and 0.549 Giga Multiply-Accumulate operations (GMAC), making it up to 10 times faster, requires 79 times less GMAC than UNet, and has 22 times fewer parameters than SegNet. These characteristics make it well-suited for deployment in clinical settings where computational resources are limited and decrease the cost of utilizing such a system. Additionally, the explainable AI technique of Grad-CAM is used to provide visual interpretability of the model's predictions and to identify regions where segmentation performance requires improvement.
authors: Sharan Thummagunti, Aayushi Padia, Abhiram Koppuravuri, Prabhu Prasad B M, G N Girish
bullets: Targets the high computational cost and slow inference of deep learning models for lung tumor segmentation.
Combines ENet with UNet-style skip connections and lightweight CBAM attention for efficient feature reuse and representation.
Trained on TCIA/MSD data and evaluated on the LIDC-IDRI dataset.
Achieves a DSC of 0.90812 with 430,052 parameters and 0.549 GMAC.
Uses Grad-CAM to interpret predictions and identify regions needing segmentation improvement.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a lightweight, energy-efficient segmentation model with drastically reduced parameters and FLOPs, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: Energy Efficient Lung Tumor Segmentation with a modified CBAM ENet Skip Model
papers.tldr: A compact ENet-based lung tumor segmentation model with CBAM and skip connections achieves strong segmentation accuracy while substantially reducing computational cost for resource-constrained clinical deployment.

papers.abstract: Marine video understanding is crucial for a wide range of real-world applications. However, existing marine video datasets suffer from limitations, including the limited number of data samples, fine-grained text descriptions, and detailed visual attributes. To address these limitations, we introduce a large-scale, video-text dataset featuring rich, in-the-wild visual attributes tailored for complex marine environments. Our dataset comprises 2,000 video-text pairs annotated with 13 attributes covering up to four objects per scene, object visual/geometric properties, behaviors, environmental context, and camera motion, spanning diverse lighting conditions, times of day, and 7 countries. From these annotations, we generate 16,080 video-question pairs (12,080 multiple-choice, 4,000 open-ended). Furthermore, we benchmark both proprietary and open-source video-LLM models on video question answering and video captioning tasks. We find that (i) proprietary models often achieves superior performances; (ii) VLMs handle object motion well but struggle with complex camera motion; (iii) closed-source models struggle to perceive camera motion; and (iv) VLMs struggle to reason in static cameras.
authors: Quang-Trung Truong, Thanh-Nghia Nguyen, Phu-Phong Vo, Jaeyeon Kim, Cheng Chen, Jie Zhang, Binh-Son Hua, Duc Thanh Nguyen, Ivor Tsang, Sai-Kit Yeung
bullets: Addresses limited sample sizes, fine-grained descriptions, and visual attributes in existing marine video datasets.
Includes 2,000 video-text pairs with 13 attributes covering object properties, behaviors, environmental context, and camera motion.
Generates 16,080 question-answer pairs spanning multiple-choice and open-ended video question answering.
Covers diverse marine scenes across lighting conditions, times of day, and seven countries.
Benchmarks video-LLMs, revealing strengths in object-motion understanding but difficulties with complex camera motion and static-camera reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a video-text dataset and benchmarks video-LLMs for marine video understanding, fitting video understanding.
papers.title: MarineLife-16K: An Attribute-Rich Video-Text Dataset for Motion-Aware Marine Video Understanding
papers.tldr: MarineLife-16K is an attribute-rich marine video-text benchmark designed to evaluate motion-aware video understanding across objects, environments, and camera movements.

papers.abstract: Advertisers routinely create multiple duration variants of ads to meet marketing budgets and viewer preferences, a labor-intensive and costly process. While multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel at general video understanding, their ability to perform specialized editorial tasks remains unexplored. We introduce AdShot, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on shot selection for ad clipping. It contains 823 professionally edited ad pairs (30-sec sources and 15-sec edits) across 194 brands and 17 industries, annotated with shot-level boundaries and content features (action, emotion, information, imagery). We evaluate 13 state-of-the-art video-only MLLMs and 2 audio-visual MLLMs (7B-72B parameters) on shot selection accuracy (Precision, Recall, F1), duration constraints (15s), and content preservation, including an audio ablation. We find: (1) model architecture matters more than scale, with smaller models often matching or exceeding larger ones; performance is strongest for target ads with 6-10 shots; (2) models exhibit a mean absolute duration error of 5.39s, with most tending to overshoot the 15s target, though they can still substantially reduce human editing effort; (3) all models exhibit systematic content biases, favoring information-rich and emotion-focused shots while under-selecting action and imagery. We publicly release our benchmark to facilitate research at the intersection of multimodal AI and computational advertising.
authors: Wen Xie, Om Rastogi, Sai Siddhartha Vivek Dhir Rangoju, Gijs Overgoor, Yakov Bart, Sarah Ostadabbas
bullets: Addresses the costly, labor-intensive creation of multiple ad-duration variants.
Introduces 823 professionally edited 30-to-15-second ad pairs spanning 194 brands and 17 industries, with shot-level annotations.
Evaluates 13 video-only and 2 audio-visual MLLMs on shot selection, 15-second duration compliance, and content preservation.
Architecture appears more important than model scale; performance is strongest on ads containing 6–10 shots.
Models typically overshoot the target by 5.39 seconds on average, favor information- and emotion-rich shots, and under-select action and imagery.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for MLLMs on video shot selection, relevant to multimodal LLMs and video understanding.
papers.title: AdShot: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Video Advertisement Clipping
papers.tldr: AdShot benchmarks how well multimodal LLMs select shots to create 15-second ad edits, revealing substantial duration errors and systematic content-selection biases.

papers.abstract: During post-training, large language models (LLMs) learn value preferences from corpora that may contain imbalanced proportions of opinions associated with different demographic groups. Amplifying these imbalances may further underrepresent some groups' opinions. However, how opinion mixtures shape value preferences across post-training paths remains unclear. To answer this question, we conduct controlled experiments using post-training corpora with different opinion mixtures and five post-training paths based on SFT, DPO, and GRPO. We find that post-training amplifies opinion imbalances differently across post-training paths. Once value preferences are amplified, whether further post-training can remove them depends on both the post-training method and the opinion mixture in the corpus. More concerningly, a model's stability under interventions depends on whether further post-training changes its value preference. Moreover, these value preferences are transferred to student models even when distillation uses corpora with no explicit opinion questions. These findings suggest that both the opinion mixture in post-training corpora and the choice of post-training method should be considered when developing, evaluating, and reusing LLMs. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/ku-nlp/llm-value-preferences.
authors: Yang Liu, Shaoyang Xu, Masahiro Kaneko, Chengzhi Zhong, Wenxuan Zhang, Chenhui Chu
bullets: Imbalanced opinions in post-training corpora can be amplified, with effects differing across SFT, DPO, and GRPO paths.
Whether later post-training removes amplified preferences depends on both the method and the corpus’s opinion mixture.
Model stability under interventions is linked to whether further post-training changes its value preferences.
Value preferences can transfer to student models even when distillation data lacks explicit opinion questions.
The findings highlight opinion composition and post-training method as important factors for developing and evaluating LLMs.
papers.selection_reason: Investigates how post-training paths shape LLM value preferences, relevant to LLM development and behavior.
papers.title: How Does Post-Training Shape LLM Value Preferences?
papers.tldr: Controlled experiments show that post-training methods and opinion mixtures jointly shape, reinforce, and sometimes transfer LLM value preferences.

papers.abstract: To understand the emergence of grammatical behavior in language models, we track circuits for subject-verb number agreement in pythia-1b and ten seeds of pythia-410m across training. We find that subject-verb agreement is learned early, and is initially handled by a diffuse collection of neurons. However, after agreement behavior has stabilized, the mechanisms responsible for it continue to reorganize. The attention heads which mediate agreement often shift during training: in the case of pythia-1b, behavior is controlled by two heads early in training but by a third (different) head later. Furthermore, the circuit shrinks over training, with pythia-1b's final circuit being strikingly sparse. We take these results to be informative about how linguistic knowledge emerges and is represented in a language model.
authors: Qing Yao, Sasha Boguraev, Tiago Pimentel, Kyle Mahowald
bullets: Agreement is initially supported by a diffuse set of neurons.
The underlying mechanism continues changing even after behavioral performance stabilizes.
Attention heads mediating agreement can be replaced during training; Pythia-1B shifts from two early heads to a different later head.
The circuit shrinks over training, producing a notably sparse final circuit in Pythia-1B.
The study tracks agreement circuits across training in Pythia-1B and ten Pythia-410M seeds.
papers.selection_reason: Traces emergence and sparsification of syntactic circuits in LLMs, relevant to language foundation model internals.
papers.title: The Emergence and Sparsification of a Syntactic Circuit
papers.tldr: Subject–verb agreement emerges early in Pythia models, then reorganizes into a much sparser syntactic circuit during continued training.

papers.abstract: Visual effects are often easier to demonstrate via reference than to describe in words. We study effect-reference editing, where a reference image shows a desired visual effect and language identifies which properties should guide the edit. Existing single-pass editing techniques often fail to make fine-grained edits, resulting in unintended changes to source content or deviations from the reference effect. We introduce KINESYS, a test-time adaptation framework for effect-reference editing that combines reference-aware and source-aware feedback to transfer the desired effect while preserving the composition and content of the original shot. To ensure KINESYS can produce a diverse set of edits that preserve the source, we develop a robust optimization strategy in which the generative model is fine-tuned across multiple noise samples and optimization runs. Evaluation with VLM judges, source preservation metrics (LPIPS, TPIPS), and a user study shows that KINESYS outperforms state-of-the-art image editors in source preservation; on effect transfer, it remains competitive with Nano Banana 2 and outperforms open-weight editors.
authors: Noah Frahm, Luchao Qi, Haoze Li, Dan B Goldman, Sambit Bhattacharya, Roni Sengupta
bullets: Targets fine-grained effect-reference editing guided by both a reference image and language.
Combines reference-aware and source-aware feedback during optimization.
Fine-tunes across multiple noise samples and optimization runs to produce diverse, source-preserving edits.
Evaluations using VLM judges, preservation metrics, and a user study show stronger source preservation than existing editors.
Effect transfer is competitive with Nano Banana 2 and better than open-weight editors.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces KINESYS, a test-time adaptation framework for reference-based image editing that updates the model during inference, fitting test-time learning and multimodal LLMs.
papers.title: KINESYS: Test-Time Adaptation for Reference-Based Effect Editing in Images
papers.tldr: KINESYS uses test-time adaptation to transfer visual effects from a reference image while preserving the source image’s content and composition.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents work in scenarios with very different memory needs. A question about past conversations needs the exact facts it names, while a multi-step task needs a trace of the steps already taken together with details that the next step cannot name. Existing memories are each designed and tested for one kind of scenario. Retrieval memories such as A-Mem miss steps that the current query does not express, summaries drop exact strings, and pairing the two fixes the split of the budget in advance. We propose FlexA-Mem, a general memory that writes each unit of history once into an immutable store and renders a fresh memory for every call. The rendered memory is a compact timeline of records plus detail that a fixed rule fits into the remaining room without an LLM call. The detail is either relevant units as raw text or excerpts or the verbatim pieces that best match the query. With one store, FlexA-Mem serves both kinds of scenario. On AppWorld challenge tasks at 4k, it outperforms the second-best method by 11.5%, and on 147 unused tasks with predictions fixed in advance it outperforms A-Mem with a summary by 12.2%. On LongMemEval and LoCoMo, it matches a dedicated keyword retriever that writes no memory, while memories built on text written by an LLM fall far behind at tight budgets. Ablations show that the timeline carries AppWorld completion, whereas recovery mainly saves steps there and decides accuracy on exact facts. Code is available at https://github.com/WujiangXu/Flex-Amem
authors: Wujiang Xu, Jiaojiao Han, Xi Zhu, Qizheng Zhang, Kaiqu Liang, Yutong Yin, Kai Mei, Dimitris N. Metaxas
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between retrieval memories that miss implicit steps and summaries that lose exact facts.
Stores each history unit once in an immutable store, then renders a fresh, budget-fitting memory without an LLM call.
Combines timeline records with either relevant raw-text excerpts or verbatim query-matched pieces.
Improves over the second-best method by 11.5% on 4k AppWorld tasks and over A-Mem with summaries by 12.2% on 147 held-out tasks.
Matches a keyword retriever on LongMemEval and LoCoMo; ablations find timelines drive AppWorld completion while detail recovery supports exact-fact accuracy.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a budget-adaptive agentic memory mechanism for LLM agents, directly fitting persistent/external LLM memory.
papers.title: FlexA-Mem: Budget-Adaptive Agentic Memory for LLM Agents
papers.tldr: FlexA-Mem adapts an LLM agent’s memory to each call by combining a compact timeline with query-matched detail under a fixed budget.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (VLMs), which process both visual inputs and text queries, incur high inference costs due to the large number of visual tokens, making visual token pruning a natural approach for improving efficiency. Recent work has leveraged query information to guide token selection, often through heuristics derived from attention patterns or token dynamics. However, these approaches do not explicitly exploit the underlying structure of query-vision interactions. We address this gap by observing that the query-vision interaction matrix, naturally induced by the query and key projections already present in transformer attention, is effectively low-rank, with a small number of dominant latent interaction modes capturing query-relevant semantics. Motivated by this observation, we propose Query-Vision Decomposition (QViD), a novel training-free query-aware visual token pruning method that exploits this structure. Extensive experiments on both image and video understanding benchmarks show that QViD consistently improves performance under matched token budgets, with the largest gains appearing under aggressive compression regimes.
authors: Harshithanjani Athi, Sravan Kumar Ankireddy, Jianzhong Charlie Zhang, Hyeji Kim
bullets: Visual token counts make large VLM inference computationally expensive.
Existing query-aware pruning methods often rely on attention heuristics without modeling query–vision interaction structure explicitly.
QViD decomposes the query–vision interaction matrix into dominant latent modes that capture query-relevant semantics.
Experiments on image and video understanding benchmarks show consistent gains at matched token budgets, especially with aggressive compression.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses visual token pruning for efficiency in VLMs.
papers.title: Vision Token Pruning via Query-Vision Interaction Decomposition
papers.tldr: QViD is a training-free method that prunes visual tokens by exploiting low-rank query–vision interactions, improving VLM efficiency and performance under fixed token budgets.

papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) operating in dynamic, challenging conditions such as intersections and roundabouts must guarantee collision avoidance under uncertainty while maintaining real-time feasibility. Most existing planners struggle to simultaneously guarantee both requirements. Chance-constrained formulations embed safety constraints directly in the optimization but become infeasible as uncertainty compounds; deterministic planners provide feasible solutions but fail to address the uncertainty that causes collisions; end-to-end learned policies provide neither guarantee in an interpretable form. We present a modular perception-prediction-planning pipeline that closes this gap by propagating uncertainty as structured, interpretable quantities across module boundaries. Rather than embedding probabilistic risk directly in the optimization, our pipeline resolves collision probabilities upstream and constructs convex safe sets within which the planner provides a guaranteed feasible solution at every cycle -- decoupling the safety guarantee from solver feasibility. Across Monte Carlo trials in a four-way unsignalized intersection, our pipeline achieves 0% collisions and 0% solver infeasibility at 12.7ms per cycle, compared to 36% and 10% collision rates for deterministic and chance-constrained baselines respectively. The ablation study confirms the necessity of each uncertainty source and the hardware deployment on Clearpath Jackal UGVs validates the pipeline's real-time viability on physical platforms.
authors: Doris Xu, Jin Hyun Park, Guadalupe Alvarado Fernandez, Adhyan Prasad, Mark Campbell
bullets: Targets safe, feasible autonomous driving in uncertain dynamic scenarios such as intersections and roundabouts.
Propagates structured uncertainty through modular perception, prediction, and planning components.
Resolves collision probabilities upstream and builds convex safe sets for a guaranteed feasible planner solution each cycle.
In four-way unsignalized-intersection Monte Carlo trials, it reported 0% collisions, 0% solver infeasibility, and 12.7 ms per cycle.
Ablations and Clearpath Jackal UGV deployment support the importance of the uncertainty sources and real-time physical viability.
papers.selection_reason: Uncertainty-aware perception-prediction-planning pipeline for collision avoidance in autonomous vehicles; directly relevant to robot navigation and obstacle avoidance.
papers.title: Interpretable Collision Avoidance and Feasibility Guarantees through an Uncertainty Aware Pipeline
papers.tldr: An interpretable uncertainty-aware AV pipeline separates collision-risk handling from planning to guarantee both collision avoidance and feasible real-time solutions.

papers.abstract: Rapid illumination transitions can disturb Visual SLAM (VSLAM) by saturating images before the Automatic Exposure (AE) policy adapts, removing the visual correspondences needed to maintain tracking. Our proposed methods mitigate this disturbance at two levels: B-Adapt acquires adaptive exposure brackets to cover the scene dynamic range while promoting photometric overlap, and BVSLAM directly uses the multi-exposure sequence as constraints in a factor graph state estimator without relying on High Dynamic Range (HDR) merging. We evaluate both methods against state-of-the-art approaches in nominal environments and during a repeated tunnel-exit transition at an emulated vehicle speed of 32 m s-1. In the tunnel, combining our B-Adapt with BVSLAM reduces the state estimation error by 78 % compared with AE images. These results suggest that bracketing efficiently improves visual pose estimation robustness to rapid illumination disturbances while retaining low error under nominal conditions. Our code is available at https://github.com/norlab-ulaval/bracketing-shows-the-way.
authors: Olivier Gamache, Anthony Lavertu, David-Alexandre Duclos, Jean-Michel Fortin, Fran\c{c}ois Pomerleau, Philippe Gigu\`ere
bullets: Rapid illumination transitions can saturate images and disrupt visual correspondences needed for tracking.
B-Adapt captures adaptive exposure brackets that cover scene brightness while preserving photometric overlap.
BVSLAM incorporates the multi-exposure sequence directly into a factor-graph estimator.
In a repeated tunnel-exit test at 32 m/s, combining B-Adapt and BVSLAM reduced state-estimation error by 78% versus automatic-exposure images.
The approach also maintained low error in nominal environments.
papers.selection_reason: Robust visual SLAM via adaptive multi-exposure bracketing for robots under illumination transitions; relevant to embodied perception, though not a core configured subtopic.
papers.title: Bracketing Shows the Way: Adaptive Multi-Exposure Policy as Input for Robust Visual SLAM
papers.tldr: Adaptive multi-exposure bracketing improves Visual SLAM robustness during rapid lighting changes without requiring HDR image merging.

papers.abstract: We present RAIWAY, an in-house wheeled bipedal robot with 20-inch wheels, together with a contact-informed control approach for rolling locomotion across irregular and discontinuous terrain.
